# ADR 0005: The collector is armed from day one, on the cron

- **Status:** Accepted; point 4's sweep fraction removed by
  [ADR 0017](0017-the-collector-refuses-on-blindness-not-on-scale.md)
- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Context doc:** [../../CLAUDE.md](../../CLAUDE.md) §1; [../testing/workerd.md](../testing/workerd.md)

## Context

The previous deployment had a mark/sweep design it never enforced in production: turning deletion on was a separate operation from deploying the cache, and it stayed off.
The bill was the small cost; the staleness was the real one, since
nothing enforced that dead paths ever leave, so the cache's semantics drifted
from "what projects need" to "everything CI ever built."

The design constraint that shaped the implementation: a deployment's
inventory can exceed one invocation's budget, and Cloudflare caps
worker CPU-time, subrequests, and wall time. A correct collector must
survive partial progress, and a safe one must refuse to sweep when the
mark phase's inputs are suspect.

## Decision

1. The collector runs on the worker's cron trigger (`0 5 * * *`),
   armed by default: `CACHET_GC_ARMED=0` disarms, everything else
   sweeps. Arming is not an operator decision point.
2. One invocation advances the run as far as a budget of 900 binding
   operations and a 13-minute headroom allow, then persists a cursor
   document into the bucket and exits cleanly. The next tick resumes
   exactly there. A run of any inventory size completes over N ticks.
3. Stages recompute at every boundary from bucket truth: inventory and
   leases never persist across ticks; mark/collect/sweep progress does,
   as cursor state.
4. The gate tripped by an unparseable lease, an unreadable root, or a
   truncated enumeration aborts the run and lands a report naming the
   gate. Nothing is deleted when the inputs are not whole. (This point
   also named a sweep fraction over 25% of inventory; ADR 0017 removed
   it, because a gate on how much a run may delete could not be
   satisfied by the run after it.)
5. Narinfos delete before their NARs, in batches, so a narinfo never
   dangles a missing NAR at any instant. Orphan NARs (referenced by no
   narinfo) survive; that is a v2 decision, guarded now by the grace
   window rather than by a bound on the sweep's size.
6. Every run lands a report at `gc-reports/{runId}.json` plus a
   `latest.json`, and the admin API serves the history.

## Consequences

Deployments get deletion with no operational surface: the cron arrives
provisioned, the first night's run sweeps what the grace window allows,
and a halt mid-run is normal operation, not an incident. The budget
split (recomputed reads vs. frozen plan state) costs some duplicate
bucket reads on multi-tick runs, accepted for resumability without
trust in persisted enumeration.

## Alternatives considered

Single-invocation sweeps with no cursor (the old design): fails open at
scale: the run dies at a platform limit and the next run starts over;
rejected. Deletion behind a manual flag or an external runner: the old
failure mode institutionalized; rejected. Sweeping orphan NARs in v1:
an inventory-level claim the mark phase cannot cheaply prove; rejected
for v1's shape.

# The cachet console

## Progress

- [x] Phase 1a-1i: the counter route (buckets, filters, write bytes,
      whoami, session scope, schemas, the account-id binding)
- [x] Phase 1 addendum: the HUD strip (public config identity, health
      route, cron parser, build stamp)
- [x] Phase 1f: the lane binds the dataset and asserts the answering path
- [x] Phase 2: assets, the console route, the lane's routing law, ADR 0014
- [x] Phase 3: the console itself (web/, five screens, the states, the
      console lane)
- [x] Phase 4: docs/console.md, README, CLAUDE.md, the integration lane's
      console and cache-miss steps

## Context

The Paper file `Nox / Cachet · Console` holds five finished 1440x900 screens:
Overview, Garbage collection, Access, Traffic, and Laptops. Nothing in the
repository serves them. There is no `.tsx`, no `.css`, no `.html`, and no
bundler config anywhere, the only `package.json` outside the generated worker
build directory is `infra/`, and the worker answers `GET /` with an RFC 9457
`not_found`.

Most of the plumbing is already in place. `require_admin`
(`crates/cachet-worker/src/verdict.rs:501`) accepts `ReadIdentity::Session`,
so a browser that finished the OAuth flow can already call all four
`/api/self/*` routes; the session cookie is HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax on
`Path=/`, which works when the console is served from the worker's own origin
and fails anywhere else. CLAUDE.md §1 and `crates/cachet-worker/src/api.rs:2`
both call the console "the future SPA". This is that work.

Four gaps sit between the screens and the data. Two are in the counter route:
`/api/self/events` groups by `kind|outcome|actor|repository|reference|project`
with no time bucket, so the per-day lines on Traffic and Laptops have no query
behind them, and it takes no filter, so "laptop reads by outcome", which is
the whole Laptops screen, cannot be asked. The third is in the writer:
Overview's "Pushed this week, 1,904 paths, 17.8 GB" wants bytes per write, and
`count_write` (`crates/cachet-worker/src/lib.rs:286`) never calls
`.measuring(...)`, so every write point carries `double2 = 0`. The fourth is
identity: no route tells a browser who it is, so a console can only learn
whether it is an admin by receiving a 403.

Underneath all four sits a binding bug that makes the counter route
unanswerable. `crates/cachet-worker/src/api.rs:142` reads
`env.var("CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID")` on every request, and `infra/alchemy.run.ts`
never binds it: a grep for `ACCOUNT_ID` across `infra/` returns nothing. So
`GET /api/self/events` answers 503 `storage_unavailable` on every deployment,
including one that sets `CACHET_DEPLOY_STATS_TOKEN`, and has done since the
route shipped in #24. The counting works, because `CACHET_EVENTS` is bound;
the reporting has never once run.

The reason nobody noticed is the second half of the same gap. The successful
path of that route has no test coverage of any kind. `workerd/wrangler.toml`
binds no Analytics Engine dataset and sets none of `CACHET_STATS_TOKEN`,
`CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, or `CACHET_STATS_DATASET`, so all six lane rows
(`workerd/check.mjs:1868`) are refused at the config check before any query
runs, and `stats::emit` returns early at `crates/cachet-worker/src/stats.rs:22`
in every scenario. `run_stats_sql`, the `SqlRow` deserialization, the response
shaping, and the whole writer path are untested, and every chart in the
console would ride all of them.

## Decisions taken

The console is served by the deployment itself, from the worker's own origin,
with the Rust router as the only authority over paths. `GET /` redirects to
`/console`, and the console lives under that prefix.

The stack is chosen for craft rather than for a small dependency count: React
19, TanStack Router, TanStack Query, StyleX, Base UI, and motion, matching the
lynk dashboard's caliber so the two consoles read as related work. Effect's
`Schema` decodes both the wire and the URL search parameters, because the
console's vocabulary and the worker's closed enums should be the same
vocabulary.

Licensed faces load from your own CDN behind a flag that defaults to off. The
repository ships Geist Mono and Geist, and a deployment that sets the flag
gets Berkeley Mono and Neue Haas Grotesk Display Pro instead.

The browser session becomes see-only. It authenticates the console's surface
and is refused on the paths that serve cache bytes, which it can reach today.

## Phase 1: the counter route answers time and filtered questions

Everything here lands before the console starts, so the console builds against
a route that works and is tested.

### 1a. Time buckets

`crates/cachet-core/src/stats_query.rs` gains two variants on the existing
`QueryDimension` enum, `Hour` and `Day`, so `by=day` reads the way you
described it. A time variant differs from a blob variant in three ways, and
all three live in the same file:

- `column()` returns a time projection (`toStartOfHour(timestamp)` or
  `toStartOfDay(timestamp)`) rather than a blob name. Confirm the exact
  function against Cloudflare's Analytics Engine SQL reference during
  implementation; `intDiv(toUInt32(timestamp), 3600) * 3600` is the fallback
  that is certain to parse.
- The ordering becomes `ORDER BY dimension ASC`, because a chart reads left to
  right, where a dimension list reads largest first.
- The `LIMIT` becomes the bucket count the window implies rather than
  `STATS_ROWS_MAX`, and it stays an integer literal from an enum.

The pair `(bucket, window)` is itself validated: `hour` is admissible only
with `window=day` (24 buckets), and `day` with `week` (7) or `month` (30).
`by=hour&window=month` would ask for 720 rows against a cap of 100, so it
answers 400 `malformed_query` rather than silently truncating a series.

Analytics Engine returns no row for a bucket with no events, and a line chart
with a missing day is a lie, so the worker fills the gaps. Filling is pure
logic over `now` and the window, so it belongs in `cachet-core` beside the
query builder, and it gives the property lane a law: a bucketed answer always
carries exactly the expected number of rows, ascending, with no gaps and no
duplicates.

One constraint worth writing down where the code can see it. The platform
stamps the `timestamp` column at ingest, and the worker cannot set it:
`worker-sys-0.8.5`'s `writeDataPoint` takes indexes, doubles, and blobs and
nothing else. So `UnixMillis now` is not the `timestamp` column, points cannot
be replayed at chosen times, and the fill must align `now` down to a bucket
boundary rather than assume the two clocks agree.

### 1b. Filters drawn from the same closed enums

Three optional query parameters join the route: `actor=`, `kind=`, and
`outcome=`. Each parses into a closed enum or refuses, and each becomes one
`AND blob{n} = '{literal}'` clause, so the threat model's claim that no caller
text reaches SQL stays literally true.

Supporting that means promoting two writer-side vocabularies from `&'static
str` to enums in `crates/cachet-core/src/stats.rs`:

- `StatKind`: `Narinfo, Nar, Part, Begin, Complete, Abort, Probe, Lease, Sweep,
  Unknown`.
- `StatOutcome`: `EdgeHit, BucketHit, Miss, Stored, Answered, Status(u16)`,
  where `Status` renders as three digits and parses only three digits.

That refactor pays a second debt. Today nothing mechanically ties
`StatPoint::blobs()`'s column order to `QueryDimension::column()`'s mapping,
and `crates/cachet-core/src/stats.rs:253` names the risk in a comment. With
both sides speaking enums, one test can assert the round trip instead of two
tests asserting halves.

`repository`, `reference`, and `project` stay unfilterable. Their values are
open strings, and admitting one would put caller text into a statement that
runs with the deployment's Cloudflare token. ADR 0015 records the choice so a
later reader knows it was a decision.

### 1c. `by=project` stops being a question with no answer

`StatPoint::for_project` (`crates/cachet-core/src/stats.rs:194`) has no call
site outside its own unit test, so `blob6` is always the empty string and
`by=project` can only ever return one empty row. The lease name is the
repository with a hyphen, which `blob4` already carries, so the dimension is
redundant rather than unimplemented. Remove `Project` from `QueryDimension`
and remove `for_project`, leaving `blob6` reserved and empty with a `// why:`
comment, because renumbering the columns would misread every point already
written.

### 1d. Writes count their bytes

`count_write` gains a byte count read from the request's `content-length` at
the router, where `write_kind` already reads the branch. The definition is
bytes that crossed the wire on this request: the compressed NAR on a whole
PUT, the part on a part PUT, and zero for begin, complete, and abort. That is
what the bucket gained, and it is the number Overview's "17.8 GB" means. The
`double2` row in DEPLOY.md's column table says so.

### 1e. The deployment binds what the counter route reads

The route reads three configuration values and the deployment supplies two.
`infra/alchemy.run.ts:56` sets `CACHET_STATS_DATASET` and, when configured,
`CACHET_STATS_TOKEN`, and never sets `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, which
`crates/cachet-worker/src/api.rs:142` reads on every request. Bind it beside
the other two.

The account id is an identifier rather than a credential, and it keeps its
unprefixed name for the reason DEPLOY.md already gives: it is the variable
every Cloudflare tool in the shell reads. `infra/src/config.ts` learns it from
`process.env.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, the same variable the deploy already
requires for alchemy's own authentication.

A stats token with no account id is a deployment that counts and silently
cannot report, so `loadStageConfig` refuses that pair by name. That file's
stated law is that a deploy which cannot configure itself fails before
touching the account, and this is exactly such a case.

### 1f. The lane binds the dataset and finally sees a 200

`workerd/wrangler.toml` gains an `[[analytics_engine_datasets]]` block for
`CACHET_EVENTS`, which alone moves `stats::emit` from an early return to its
real path in every scenario: the builder construction and the blob and double
marshalling start running under test. Confirm miniflare accepts the binding
type when wiring it; if it refuses, the writer's coverage stays in the unit
lane and the doc says so rather than implying a coverage the lane does not
have.

The read side needs one more seam. `run_stats_sql` hardcodes
`https://api.cloudflare.com/...`, so no test can reach its success path. Give
the base URL a variable, `CACHET_STATS_API_URL`, exactly as `CACHET_JWKS_URL`
and `CACHET_GITHUB_API_URL` already work, and point it at the workerd driver's
stub server alongside the lane's `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`,
`CACHET_STATS_DATASET`, and a `CACHET_STATS_TOKEN` entering through
`.dev.vars` the way the signing secret already does.

The stub earns more than one assertion. It receives the composed SQL as a
plain text body, so it can assert the statement byte-for-byte before answering
canned rows, which turns the query builder into a wire-level contract in place
of the four substring assertions it has today. With that in place the lane
covers, for the first time: the 200 path, `SqlRow` deserialization, the
response shaping, the zero fill, the emitted SQL for each subject, dimension,
window, and filter combination, and the refusal of an inadmissible
`(bucket, window)` pair. The existing 503 rows stay, moved to a scenario that
deliberately unsets the token, so "counts but cannot report" remains a tested
answer rather than becoming an accident.

### 1g. `GET /api/whoami`

The console needs to know who it is before it renders anything. The route sits
outside `/api/self/` because it must answer for an org member who is not an
admin, and `/api/self/*` is admin-gated by documented contract.

```json
{ "login": "shivansh", "admin": true, "credential": "browser",
  "expiresAtMs": 1789000000000 }
```

`credential` comes from the `ReadIdentity` variant (`browser`, `laptop`, or
`ci`), and `expiresAtMs` is present only for a session. An unauthenticated
request answers 401, which the console reads as "show the sign-in screen"
rather than as an error.

### 1h. A browser session stops being a cache-read credential

A session cookie reads cache contents today. `read_routes`
(`crates/cachet-worker/src/lib.rs:343`) authorizes narinfo and NAR reads
through `verdict::authorize_read`, which accepts the cookie and answers
`ReadIdentity::Session` with no scope attached, and nothing downstream
distinguishes that identity from a laptop's. Meanwhile `resolve_session`
(`crates/cachet-worker/src/verdict.rs:400`) checks only that the record is
younger than its 14-day TTL, so it never re-checks org membership. The two
facts together mean a copy of an ex-member's cookie substitutes from the cache
for a fortnight after they leave the org.

Give the session identity a scope: it authenticates the console's own surface
(`/api/self/*`, `/api/whoami`, `/api/probe` for the search field, and
`/roots`) and is refused on the object paths that serve cache bytes. Nix never
sends a cookie, so nothing legitimate loses a credential, and the browser
becomes see-only in fact rather than by assumption. The refusal is
`ClientError::Unauthorized`, the same answer an anonymous read gets, and the
workerd lane asserts it on both a narinfo and a NAR.

The statistics window then stands as an accepted trade: a session outlives org
removal by up to 14 days for counters and GC reports, and
`docs/security/threat-model.md:64` gets corrected to say that rather than
claiming a 600s verdict re-check the code never performs.

Closing the statistics window too would mean storing the GitHub token on the
session record and re-checking membership the way ADR 0002 already does for
laptops. That is a second GitHub credential at rest in KV for a window you
have judged acceptable, so this plan does not take it. ADR 0016 records both
the scope and the trade, so the choice is legible later.

### 1i. The two verbatim bodies get schemas

`GET /api/self/gc-runs/{runId}` and `GET /roots/{project}` stream stored JSON
verbatim, so `crates/cachet-api/src/routes.rs:435` declares them as untyped
`application/json` and the OpenAPI document describes their bodies not at all.
A typed console client wants both. Declare `GcReport` and `LeaseDocument` as
mirror schemas in `cachet-api` with a unit test asserting each mirror
round-trips the core type's JSON, because deriving `utoipa::ToSchema` on
`cachet-core` would put a derive macro dependency inside the pure crate and
cross §4's boundary.

## Phase 2: the deployment serves the console

### 2a. The asset binding

`infra/alchemy.run.ts` gains one property on the existing `Cloudflare.Worker`
resource. The installed alchemy (2.0.0-beta.74) already supports it;
`infra/node_modules/alchemy/src/Cloudflare/Workers/Worker.ts:704` documents
`assets` and `runWorkerFirst`, and confirm the exact `AssetsProps` field names
there rather than from the website docs.

```ts
assets: {
  directory: "../web/dist",
  // why: the Rust router is the only authority over paths. An asset rule
  // that answered a /{hash}.narinfo miss with index.html would serve every
  // nix substituter 200 text/html where it expects a 404.
  runWorkerFirst: true,
},
```

`bundle: false` and `main: ../crates/cachet-worker/build/index.js` stay as they
are. Assets upload beside the wasm bundle; rolldown never sees either.

### 2b. The Rust side

A new `crates/cachet-worker/src/console.rs` owns two functions and the router
gains one branch ahead of the protocol paths:

- `owns(path)` answers true for `/console` and anything under `/console/`.
- `serve(env, req, path)` fetches from `env.assets("ASSETS")` (workers-rs
  0.8.5 has `Env::assets`), and rewrites a path with no file extension to
  `/console/index.html` so a deep link into the router serves the shell.
- `GET /` answers 302 to `/console`.

A deployment whose worker predates the binding must degrade rather than fail:
a missing `ASSETS` binding answers 404 for `/console`, exactly as today. That
mirrors the stats binding's existing contract, where a worker older than the
dataset counts nothing and serves exactly as well.

### 2c. The lane proves the law

`workerd/wrangler.toml` gains an `[assets]` block pointing at a small
committed fixture directory, `workerd/fixtures/assets/`, holding an
`index.html` and one hashed file. The fixture keeps `just workerd` free of a
Vite build, and the real bundle's serving is proven live by the integration
lane instead.

The new scenario asserts, in one boot: `/` redirects to `/console`; `/console`
serves the shell; `/console/traffic` serves the shell; `/console/assets/x.js`
serves the file with its own content type; `/nix-cache-info` is unchanged; and
**a `/{hash}.narinfo` read for an absent path still answers 404 problem+json
with assets bound**. That last row is the one that matters, and it is the
reason the routing decision lives in Rust.

### 2d. The callback stops needing configuration

`CACHET_UI_ORIGIN` is today the verbatim `Location` of the post-login 302, and
a deployment that leaves it unset answers 204 instead
(`crates/cachet-core/src/oauth.rs:131`). With the console at the deployment's
own host, the default becomes `https://{CACHET_HOST}/console`, so the browser
flow works with no operator configuration at all. Keep the variable as an
override for anyone hosting a UI elsewhere, and update the DEPLOY.md row and
`scripts/bootstrap.sh`'s generated env file to say what it now means.

## Phase 3: the console

### 3a. The workspace

A `web/` directory at the repository root, built by bun and Vite, both already
in the devshell (`nix/devshell.nix` carries `pkgs.bun` and `pkgs.nodejs_22`).
`bun.lock` commits, and the build runs `bun install --frozen-lockfile` the way
`just deploy` already does for `infra/`.

Runtime dependencies, each with the `// why:` comment §6 requires, in the
`package.json`:

| Package | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `react`, `react-dom` | The view layer. |
| `@tanstack/react-router` | Typed routes and typed search parameters, so a filtered Traffic view is a link someone can send. SPA mode; no TanStack Start, because the worker serves static assets and an SSR entry would collide with `main: build/index.js`. |
| `@tanstack/react-query` | Polling, caching, and refetch on focus for a dashboard that reads six routes. |
| `@stylexjs/stylex`, `@stylexjs/unplugin` | Atomic styles compiled at build time, with the design tokens as the only source of scale values. |
| `@base-ui/react` | Headless primitives for the segmented controls, menus, and tooltips the screens use. |
| `motion` | The counter and chart transitions that make the console feel alive rather than repainted. |
| `effect` | `Schema` decodes API responses and URL search parameters through the same closed vocabulary the Rust enums define. Pinned to the exact version `infra/` already pins. |
| `@fontsource-variable/geist`, `-geist-mono` | The shipped faces, both OFL. |

Vite builds with `base: "/console/"` to `web/dist`.

### 3b. Tokens and fonts

`web/src/styles/tokens.stylex.ts` carries the Paper file's token values
verbatim: the `--color-*` set, the `--text-*` scale, `--font-weight-*`,
`--tracking-*`, `--leading-*`, and the spacing scale. Each font stack names
the licensed face first and the shipped one behind it:

```
--font-mono:    "Berkeley Mono", "Geist Mono", ui-monospace, monospace
--font-display: "Neue Haas Grotesk Display Pro", "Geist", system-ui, sans-serif
```

The flag is one optional stylesheet. `/api/public/config` gains a nullable
`fontCss` field sourced from a new `CACHET_FONT_CSS` variable
(`CACHET_DEPLOY_FONT_CSS` in the deploy contract), and the console appends a
single `<link rel="stylesheet">` when it is present. With the flag off, which
is the default, the licensed families resolve to nothing and Geist Mono
renders. With it on, the CDN's `@font-face` rules make them resolve. Nothing
about the bundle changes between the two, so deployment identity stays
configuration (ADR 0010) and no licensed byte enters the repository.

The console asking a third-party origin for fonts is a new fact about its
trust surface, so `docs/security/threat-model.md` gains a sentence naming it
and the default-off posture.

### 3c. The screens

The shell is shared by all five and matches the Paper structure: a `hud-strip`
across the top, a 64px `rail` of navigation icons, a `header` carrying the
breadcrumb and the search field, the `content` region, and a `status-bar`
naming the signed-in login and the host.

Each screen's data sources, all of which exist after phase 1:

| Screen | Reads |
| --- | --- |
| Overview | `/api/self/stats`, `/api/self/gc-runs` for the 30-run line, `/api/self/events?subject=reads&window=week`, `?subject=writes&by=repository&window=week` |
| Garbage collection | `/api/self/gc-runs`, `/api/self/gc-runs/{runId}` |
| Access | `/api/public/config`, `/api/whoami`, `POST /logout` |
| Traffic | `/api/self/events` with `subject` from the Reads/Writes/Probes control, `window` from Day/Week/Month, `by=hour|day` for the line and `by=outcome` for the table |
| Laptops | `/api/self/events?subject=reads&actor=laptop` grouped by `day` and by `outcome`, plus the unfiltered read total for the share |

Charts are hand-rolled SVG. The Paper file's chart is one area path, one line
path, one gridline, and an endpoint circle
(`panel-chart` under the Traffic artboard), so a charting library would carry
weight nothing here needs. The scales are pure functions in
`web/src/lib/`, which is where the console lane tests them.

Follow the repository's own convention for structure: route files do the
wiring, presentational components take props and no queries, and derivations
live in pure modules. That split is what makes the lane's component tests
possible without a mock framework.

### 3d. States the mockups do not cover

Six states need design before they need code, and each one is reachable today:

- **Signed out.** `/api/whoami` answers 401. The console shows a sign-in
  screen pointing at `/_auth/login`.
- **Org member who is not an admin.** `admin: false`. Access renders; the
  other four screens are hidden with a line naming `CACHET_ADMINS` as the
  reason.
- **Loading.** Skeletons rather than spinners, gated so a fast answer never
  flashes one.
- **Fresh deployment.** `/api/self/stats` answers 404 by design when no
  collection has finished (`crates/cachet-worker/src/api.rs:345`). Overview
  and Garbage collection must read that as "no run yet", never as an error.
- **Counting without reporting.** A deployment with no `CACHET_STATS_TOKEN`
  answers 503 `storage_unavailable` on `/api/self/events`. Traffic and Laptops
  must say that the deployment counts but cannot report, and point at the
  DEPLOY.md row.
- **A tripped GC gate.** `gate` is non-null on the run, which the Garbage
  collection screen already shows in red for one row; the same treatment
  belongs on Overview when the latest run tripped.

### 3e. The console lane

Per §9 every test belongs to exactly one lane, and a lane's id is its just
verb, its CI job, and its doc basename. The new lane is `console`:

1. `docs/testing/console.md`
2. `[lane.console]` with a summary in `docs/testing/lanes.toml`
3. `@docs/testing/console.md` in CLAUDE.md §11
4. `console:` in the justfile, running vitest
5. a `console:` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` whose steps run
   `just console`

All five land in one commit, which is what `scripts/check-lane-manifest.sh`
enforces in both directions.

The lane covers the pure derivations (chart scales, byte and count formatting,
the search-parameter codecs, the Schema decoders against recorded response
bodies) and the presentational components under Testing Library with injected
props. The build verb is separate and named `web`, the way `just wasm` is the
build and `just workerd` is the lane.

## Phase 4: the documents catch up

Four ADRs and five documents, following `docs/adr/README.md`'s format. The
next free number is 0014.

- **ADR 0014, the console is served by the deployment.** Why the same worker
  and the same origin (the session cookie is SameSite=Lax and no CORS layer
  exists), why `run_worker_first` is true rather than a glob list (a protocol
  path added later must not be able to start serving the app shell), and why
  `/console` rather than the root.
- **ADR 0015, the counters answer time and filtered questions.** Why the
  bucket joins the dimension enum, why `(bucket, window)` pairs are validated,
  why filters are limited to closed enums, and why the SQL API's base URL
  became a variable.
- **ADR 0016, the browser session is see-only.** A refinement of ADR 0002,
  recording that a session authenticates the console's surface and is refused
  on cache object reads, and that the 14-day statistics window is an accepted
  trade rather than an oversight.
- **`docs/console.md`**, the console's own document: what each screen answers,
  which route each panel reads, and the states listed in 3d. One
  `@docs/console.md` line in CLAUDE.md §11, unfenced and unbackticked, or
  `scripts/check-doc-manifest.sh` fails on the fourth assertion.
- **`docs/DEPLOY.md`**: a console section, the `CACHET_DEPLOY_FONT_CSS` row,
  the corrected `CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN` row, the `double2`-for-writes
  definition, the new query parameters on `/api/self/events`, and a
  `CACHET_DEPLOY_STATS_TOKEN` row saying that reporting needs
  `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` in the deploy environment as well, because the
  worker now carries it.
- **`docs/security/threat-model.md`**: the corrected session sentence, the
  console's origin, and the third-party font CDN.
- **`README.md`**: an admin section beside the laptop and CI ones.
- **`CLAUDE.md`**: §1's "the future SPA" becomes the console, and §4 names

## Verification

Run the local gates in the order the phases land. `just check` is the
pre-push parity verb, though note it does not currently run `workerd`, so run
that one by hand.

```
nix develop
just unit property golden
just openapi && just openapi-check
just wasm && just workerd
just web && just console
just check
```

Then prove the console end to end against a real deployment. Staging deploys
automatically after a green `ci` on main, so the fastest path is a merge; to
rehearse locally instead:

```
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=... CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=... just deploy cachet-staging
CACHET_INTEGRATION_URL=https://<staging host> just integration
```

Before the browser checks, confirm the binding fix on the deployment itself,
because this is the first time the route can answer at all:

```
curl -sS --netrc-file ~/.netrc \
  "https://<staging host>/api/self/events?subject=reads&by=day&window=week"
```

It answers 200 with seven rows in ascending date order, zeros included. A 503
`storage_unavailable` means the account id still is not reaching the worker.

By hand in a browser, against staging, confirm each of these:

1. `https://<host>/` redirects to `/console`, and an unauthenticated visit
   shows the sign-in screen rather than a 401 body.
2. Sign-in through GitHub lands back on `/console` with the session cookie
   set, and the status bar names your login.
3. All five screens render with live numbers, and Traffic's Day, Week, and
   Month controls each change the line's bucket count to 24, 7, and 30.
4. Laptops shows a non-zero share, which proves the cross-filter reached the
   query.
5. `curl -s https://<host>/<some absent hash>.narinfo` still answers 404
   `application/problem+json`, and `nix copy --from https://<host>` still
   substitutes a pushed path. This is the assertion the whole serving design
   exists to protect, and the integration lane's step 5 already covers the
   second half.
6. A second GitHub account that is an org member but absent from
   `CACHET_ADMINS` sees Access and nothing else.
7. Copy your `cachet_session` cookie out of the browser and replay it against
   a narinfo path. It answers 401, and the same cookie still answers
   `/api/self/stats`.

The integration lane gains one step for the first and fifth of those, so the
round trip is proven by `just integration` rather than by memory.

worker knows its host and not its name, so `infra/alchemy.run.ts` binds
`CACHET_DEPLOY_NAME` from the stage it already computes, and
`/api/public/config` grows `deployment`, `version`, and `buildSha`. Version
comes from `env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")`. The build sha comes from
`option_env!("CACHET_BUILD_SHA")`, which the `wasm` recipe sets from
`git rev-parse --short=6 HEAD` before calling worker-build, so a plain
`cargo build` leaves it absent rather than lying.

`UTC 05:14:02` needs no route. Every response already carries a `Date`
header, so the console takes its offset from the last answer and ticks
locally. That shows the deployment's clock rather than the laptop's, which
is what a HUD beside a deployment name means.

`NEXT COLLECTION IN 23 H 46 M` and `● HEALTHY` come from a new admin route,
`GET /api/self/health`, answering `status`, `nextCollectionAtMs`,
`latestRunId`, `latestFinishedAtMs`, and `gate`. The cron expression lives in
the alchemy program alone, so it binds as `CACHET_GC_CRON` and a total parser
in `cachet-core` recognizes the daily `M H * * *` shape and answers the next
UTC instant, or answers nothing for any other shape so the console hides the
countdown rather than inventing one. Status is derived: `healthy` when the
latest report exists, tripped no gate, and finished within two cron periods;
`degraded` when it tripped a gate or is older than that; `unknown` on a
deployment with no report yet.

The split matters for a non-admin. Identity and the clock ride
`/api/public/config` and the `Date` header, which an org member can read, so
their HUD renders with the countdown and the status dot omitted rather than
the strip failing.

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_editor_state(include_schema: true) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.

Tools: get_editor_state, get_guidelines, batch_get, batch_design, snapshot_layout, get_screenshot, get_variables, set_variables, export_nodes.

## plugin:paper-desktop:paper
Paper is a professional design tool for creating user interfaces. The user is working on a 2D canvas composing designs.
The Paper MCP server gives you tools to be a talented designer for web and mobile apps and websites. You can read designs from the user's file, understand what the user is currently doing, and write HTML back into the design as new nodes.

You MUST load the full guide before other Paper tools: get_guide({ topic: "paper-mcp-instructions" }). Do this once per session; call again if a long thread may have compressed or dropped guide text.

- Context: call get_basic_info first to understand artboards and dimensions; use get_selection to see user focus.
- Typography: you MUST call get_font_family_info before your first typographic styling in a session. Prefer font families already listed in get_basic_info unless the user specifies otherwise. Use px for font sizes, em for letter-spacing, px for line-height.
- New designs: before writing HTML, generate a brief (palette, type scale, spacing, direction) unless the user provides a design system.
- Creating/editing: each write_html call should add roughly one visual group; prefer duplicate_nodes with update_styles and set_text_content when it is faster than rewriting HTML.
- Quality: use get_screenshot to review after meaningful changes. Artboard height is a starting point — when content clips switch the artboard to height: "fit-content" via update_styles rather than guessing fixed heights.
- Repeated rows (lists, nav): use fixed-width slots for icons and trailing actions (flexShrink: 0); do not rely on gap alone to align columns across rows.
- When done creating or editing, you MUST call finish_working_on_nodes.
- User-facing output: do not include raw node IDs.
- Export to the user's codebase: use get_jsx, get_computed_styles, get_fill_image, etc. for exact values — do not read sizes or colors from screenshots alone.

# ADR 0017: The collector refuses on blindness, not on scale

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-26
- **Context doc:** [0005-gc-on-the-cron.md](0005-gc-on-the-cron.md);
  [../security/threat-model.md](../security/threat-model.md)

## Context

The collector carried three abort gates. Two fire when it cannot see the
truth: an unreadable root narinfo or an unparseable lease means the mark
set is wrong, and a truncated enumeration means the inventory is
incomplete. The third fired on scale: a sweep whose candidate count
exceeded a quarter of the narinfo inventory aborted the run.

The third one cannot be satisfied. Aborting produces an empty deletion
plan, so nothing is deleted, so the next run enumerates the same
inventory and computes the same candidates and aborts again. The
candidate set only grows, because every path already past its grace
window stays past it. A deployment where more than a quarter of the cache
is genuinely dead stops collecting permanently, and the only exit is a
person with bucket access.

That is the wrong failure for this system twice over. A binary cache's
characteristic problem is unbounded growth, and this gate converts "a lot
is dead" into "nothing is ever collected". And the thing it protected
against is cheap here: over-deleting from a cache costs a rebuild and a
re-push, not data. The store paths still exist in every machine that
built them.

## Decision

1. The sweep fraction gate is removed, along with its constants, its
   `GateTrip` variant, and its report value.
2. The gates that remain are the ones that fire on blindness: an
   unreadable root narinfo, an unparseable lease, a truncated inventory
   or lease listing, an exhausted walk budget, and a corrupt generation
   document. Each of those means the collector's picture of what is live
   is incomplete, which is the condition worth refusing on.
3. How much one run may delete is not bounded.

## Consequences

A collection deletes everything the mark phase proved dead, however much
that is. A deployment that decommissions half its repositories collects
normally on the next tick instead of jamming.

The blast radius of a mark-phase bug widens: one that failed to mark live
paths would now sweep them. What limits it is unchanged and is the part
that was always doing the work: nothing is swept until its grace window
past the last lease that named it has passed, so a mistake needs to
survive fourteen days of nothing referencing a path. And the recovery is
a push, because that is what a cache is.

## Alternatives considered

**Keep the gate and add an override.** A variable an operator sets to let
one run through. Rejected: it makes the deadlock a thing you have to know
about and then know how to escape, and the escape is a setting nobody
reads until they are already stuck.

**Raise the fraction.** Any fixed fraction has the same deadlock at some
inventory, and picking a bigger number only moves the wall.

**Cap the deletions per run rather than refusing them.** Sweep at most N
and let successive runs drain the rest. This is a real option and would
bound a bug's damage per night while still converging. Rejected for now
because it adds a partial-sweep state to a collector whose runs are
currently whole, and the grace window already gives the same protection
in time rather than in count. Worth revisiting if a mark-phase bug ever
does happen.

  [0017-the-collector-refuses-on-blindness-not-on-scale.md](0017-the-collector-refuses-on-blindness-not-on-scale.md)

## Context

The mark phase walks from the roots the leases name. When a narinfo read
fails, the walker learns which way it failed: `Absent` means the bucket
answered that no such object is there, and `Unparseable` means the object
is there and its text does not parse. A read that fails because the
binding itself failed is neither, and freezes the run rather than
answering the walker at all.

Both failures were treated the same at a root and both tripped the
`unreadable_root_narinfo` gate, which aborts the run with nothing
deleted. Deeper in the closure the same two failures were treated the
other way: the path is marked, `unreadableDeep` counts it, and the walk
goes on.

The absent half of that has the deadlock shape ADR 0017 removed from the
sweep fraction. A lease naming a path whose narinfo is gone keeps naming
it, and nothing about a later run brings the narinfo back, so every
collection from then on aborts at the same root. Staging reached exactly
this state: every run answered "stopped at the unreadable_root_narinfo
gate, nothing was deleted", and the only exits were pushing that project
again or editing the lease by hand.

Refusing also protects nothing there. A path whose narinfo is absent is
a path no client can substitute, because a substitution starts by
fetching that narinfo. Its references cannot be enumerated, but nothing
reachable only through it is reachable at all.

The unparseable half is different, and worth keeping. That root is
present and servable: a client fetches the narinfo, gets bytes, and the
worker serves it. Its references cannot be read, so continuing would
sweep a closure whose top a client can still reach. That is blindness,
which is what ADR 0017 says a gate is for.

## Decision

1. An absent root narinfo does not gate. It is marked, so the sweep
   never touches it, and it is counted in `unreadableDeep` the same way
   an absent reference deeper in the closure has always been counted.
2. An unparseable root narinfo still trips `unreadable_root_narinfo`,
   and the run aborts with nothing deleted.
3. A read that fails because the R2 binding failed keeps freezing the
   run for the next tick, unchanged. That distinction is what makes the
   first point safe: `Absent` is the bucket's answer that the object is
   not there, never an error dressed as one.

## Consequences

A lease naming a path the cache no longer holds costs one counted
unreadable reference per run instead of stopping collection for good.
Deployments already stuck resume on the next tick with no operator
action.

`unreadableDeep` on a report now counts absent roots alongside absent
references, so a number that climbs says leases are naming paths that
left the cache. That is the signal the gate used to deliver by stopping
everything, and it is the proportionate one, because it does not also
stop the collector.

## Alternatives considered

**Drop the root gate entirely.** Treat unparseable like absent and let
the walk continue past both. Rejected: an unparseable root is servable
with references nobody can read, so continuing sweeps live paths that
clients can still reach through it.

**Delete the lease when its root is absent.** The collector repairs the
condition rather than counting it. Rejected: the collector reads leases
and does not write them, and a lease that names a path pushed again
tomorrow is not wrong, only ahead of the cache.

# ADR 0018: Only an unparseable root narinfo stops the collector

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-26
- **Context doc:** [0005-gc-on-the-cron.md](0005-gc-on-the-cron.md);
  [0017-the-collector-refuses-on-blindness-not-on-scale.md](0017-the-collector-refuses-on-blindness-not-on-scale.md)

## Context

The mark phase walks from the roots the leases name. When a narinfo read
fails, the walker learns which way it failed: `Absent` means the bucket
answered that no such object is there, and `Unparseable` means the object
is there and its text does not parse. A read that fails because the R2
binding itself failed is neither. It freezes the run for the next tick
without answering the walker at all.

Both failures were treated the same way at a root, and both tripped the
`unreadable_root_narinfo` gate, which aborts the run and deletes nothing.
Deeper in the closure the same two failures were treated the other way:
the path is marked, `unreadableDeep` counts it, and the walk goes on.

The absent case has the deadlock shape ADR 0017 removed from the sweep
fraction. A lease naming a path whose narinfo is gone keeps naming it,
and nothing about a later run brings the narinfo back, so every
collection from then on aborts at the same root. Staging reached that
state: every run answered "stopped at the unreadable_root_narinfo gate,
nothing was deleted", and the exits were pushing that project again or
editing the lease by hand.

Refusing there also protects nothing. A path whose narinfo is absent is
a path no client can substitute, because a substitution starts by
fetching that narinfo. Its references cannot be enumerated, and nothing
reachable only through it is reachable at all.

The unparseable case is different. That root is present and servable: a
client fetches the narinfo, gets bytes, and the worker answers. Its
references cannot be read, so continuing would sweep a closure whose top
a client still reaches. The collector's picture of what is live is
incomplete there, which is the condition ADR 0017 kept the remaining
gates for.

## Decision

1. An absent root narinfo does not gate. It is marked, so the sweep
   never touches it, and it is counted in `unreadableDeep` the same way
   an absent reference deeper in the closure has always been counted.
2. An unparseable root narinfo still trips `unreadable_root_narinfo`,
   and the run aborts having deleted nothing.
3. A read that fails because the R2 binding failed keeps freezing the
   run for the next tick, unchanged. That distinction is what makes the
   first point safe: `Absent` is the bucket answering that the object is
   not there, and a binding failure never reaches the walker as one.

## Consequences

A lease naming a path the cache no longer holds costs one counted
unreadable reference per run instead of stopping collection for good.
Deployments already stuck resume on the next tick with no operator
action.

`unreadableDeep` on a report now counts absent roots alongside absent
references, so a number that climbs says leases are naming paths that
left the cache. The gate used to deliver that signal by stopping
everything, and this delivers it without stopping anything.

## Alternatives considered

**Drop the root gate entirely.** Treat unparseable like absent and let
the walk continue past both. Rejected: an unparseable root is servable
with references nobody can read, so continuing sweeps live paths clients
can still reach through it.

**Delete the lease when its root is absent.** The collector repairs the
condition rather than counting it. Rejected: the collector reads leases
and never writes them, and a lease naming a path that gets pushed again
tomorrow describes a real project whose cache entry has expired.
MDEOF

git commit -q -F - <<'MSGEOF'
A lease naming a departed path stops jamming the collector

Staging's collector answered "stopped at the unreadable_root_narinfo
gate, nothing was deleted" on every run. A lease named a path whose
narinfo is no longer in the bucket, the mark phase refused, and no later
run could do anything about it: the lease keeps naming the path and
nothing brings the narinfo back. That is the deadlock ADR 0017 removed
from the sweep fraction, in a second place.

The walker already learns which way a narinfo read failed. Absent means
the bucket answered that no such object is there; unparseable means the
object is there and its text does not parse; a failed R2 binding is
neither and freezes the run without answering the walker. Only the
unparseable case gates now. That root is present and servable with
references nobody can enumerate, so continuing would sweep a closure
whose top a client still reaches. An absent root is marked, counted in
unreadableDeep, and walked past, because no client can substitute a path
whose narinfo is gone and refusing protected nothing.

The property lane gains the walk law over arbitrary root sets and read
outcomes, and the workerd lane gains the two scenarios, one per answer,
since a tripped gate ends the run and one bucket cannot show both.
ADR 0018 records it; 0005, 0017, the threat model, and the two lane docs
follow.

Also drops the explanatory paragraph from the sign-in screen.
MSGEOF

content.text:
Pushed as `4ec51ad`; CI is running.

**The gate.** `unreadable_root_narinfo` had the same permanent-refusal shape as the sweep-fraction gate we deleted: a lease naming a path whose narinfo left the bucket blocked every future collection, and no later run could clear it.

The walker already knew which way a read failed. It just didn't use it at a root:

- **Absent** — R2 answered that no such object is there. Now marked, counted in `unreadableDeep`, walked past. No client can substitute a path whose narinfo is gone, since a substitution starts by fetching that narinfo, so refusing protected nothing.
- **Unparseable** — the object is there and won't parse. Still gates. That root is servable with references nobody can enumerate, so continuing would sweep a closure whose top a client still reaches.
- **Binding failure** — never reaches the walker at all; it freezes the run for the next tick, unchanged. That's what makes treating `Absent` as authoritative safe.

Landed with its gates: the property lane's walk law over arbitrary root sets and read outcomes, two workerd scenarios (one per answer — a tripped gate ends the run, so one bucket can't show both), ADR 0018, and rows in ADR 0005, ADR 0017, the threat model, and both lane docs. Workerd is green at 104 assertions.

Two things still open from before:

1. Staging redeploys automatically after this CI run goes green, and its 05:00 UTC collection should then complete instead of tripping — which should also flip the console's health from `degraded` to `healthy`.
2. `bcbb65c`, the rejected probe-based edge commit, is still in history. Say the word if you want it squashed out.

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSGEOF'
Version 0.1.2: the collector stops jamming on a departed root

A lease naming a path whose narinfo is no longer in the bucket stopped
every collection this deployment would ever run. The mark phase refused,
and nothing about a later run could change the answer: the lease keeps
naming the path and no run brings the narinfo back. Staging sat in that
state, reporting "stopped at the unreadable_root_narinfo gate, nothing
was deleted" every night. This release ends it.

The gate now fires only where the collector is actually blind. A root
whose narinfo will not parse is present and servable with references
nobody can enumerate, so sweeping on would delete a closure whose top a
client still reaches, and that still aborts the run. A root whose
narinfo is absent is marked, counted in the report's unreadableDeep, and
walked past, because no client can substitute a path whose narinfo is
gone.

Operators upgrading from 0.1.1 need do nothing. A deployment stuck on
this gate collects again on its next tick, and a report's unreadableDeep
climbing is the signal that leases name paths the cache no longer holds.
MSGEOF

content.text:
Nothing is broken. Here's the walkthrough.

**The 6,833 isn't a real number.** The report doesn't carry a candidate count at all — the console computes it as `inventoryPaths - markedPaths`, and 7,132 − 299 = 6,833 exactly. That subtraction ignores the grace window, which is the only thing that decides what actually sweeps. So the tile says "6,833 unmarked" and reads as "6,833 about to be deleted", which is my bug in `web/src/screens/collection.tsx:142`.

**The real sweep set was zero, and correctly so.** `sweep_candidates` (`crates/cachet-core/src/gc.rs:327`) takes a path only when it's both unmarked *and* uploaded more than the grace window ago:

```rust
if !marked.contains(&hash)
    && now.saturating_ms_since(UnixMillis::new(item.uploaded_at_ms)) > grace_ms
```

Grace is 14 days on production (`GRACE_WINDOW_MS`, and DEPLOY.md keeps the default there). This repo's first commit is 21 Aug and `v0.1.0` was tagged 25 Aug — six days ago. Every object in that bucket was uploaded inside the window, so nothing was eligible. Production won't delete its first path until roughly 4 September, and then only paths no lease has named since.

There's corroborating evidence in the run itself: 2 min 19 s and a clean finish. Had the sweep set really been 6,833, the collect stage would have to read 6,833 narinfos to resolve their NAR URLs (`crates/cachet-worker/src/gc.rs:791`) against a 900-operation budget. It would have frozen a cursor on the first tick and reported "Frozen", not "Completed".

**On 25 and 26 Aug showing "Stopped":** that's the gate we just fixed. Those runs never got as far as planning. The 27 Aug run completed because somebody pushed that project again and its narinfo came back — which was the only escape from that gate before today. So the fix is still doing real work; production just hasn't hit the condition since.

The tile is genuinely misleading and I'd like to fix it. The honest options: relabel it "Unmarked", or add the grace-filtered count to the report so the console can show what would actually sweep. The second is a report schema change, so it touches the API mirror, the openapi document, and the console schema. Which do you want?

content.text:
Yes — it went sideways today, and the fix we shipped isn't the cause. Here's the whole history from production's own reports:

```
finished          dur    inv marked leases  ndel  freed  gate
25 Aug 05:01      13s   4966      0      1     0      0   unreadable_root_narinfo
26 Aug 05:00      19s   6105      0      2     0      0   unreadable_root_narinfo
27 Aug 05:02     139s   7132    299      2     0      0   None
28 Aug 05:01      80s   7309    299      2     0      0   None
29 Aug 05:01      84s   7309    299      2     0      0   None
30 Aug 05:01      83s   7309    299      2     0      0   None
31 Aug 05:01     103s  11734    299      2     0      0   None
01 Sep 05:01     103s  11734    299      2     0      0   None
02 Sep 05:02     107s  11734    299      2     0      0   None
03 Sep 05:02     112s  14064    300      3     0      0   None
04 Sep 05:02     113s  14529    300      3     0      0   None
05 Sep 05:02     102s  14529    300      3     0      0   None
06 Sep 05:02      96s  14529    300      3     0      0   None
07 Sep 05:02     107s  14634    300      3     0      0   None
```

Production has never deleted a single object. Inventory went 4,966 → 14,634. The 27 Aug–7 Sep zeros were legitimate: 14-day grace, nothing old enough. (My estimate that day of "roughly 4 September" was off; the real boundary is 8 Sep, 14 days after the 25 Aug inventory.)

**The 8 Sep run has no report, and it's 23:40 UTC.** The cron fires at 05:00, so that tick fired ~18 hours ago and produced nothing. A report only lands when a run finishes or aborts. A run that exhausts its budget parks `meta/gc-cursor`, logs `gc.paused`, and lands no report — so the missing report says the 8 Sep run is still in progress, frozen mid-run. That is exactly what the first post-grace run would do.

**Why.** The collect stage reads one narinfo per candidate to resolve its NAR URL (`crates/cachet-worker/src/gc.rs:802`) against `GC_OP_BUDGET = 900` ops per invocation. Today, everything the bucket held on 25 Aug crossed grace at once: 4,966 narinfos, 300 of them marked live, so ~4,600 became eligible simultaneously. After listing pages and the cursor round trip, a tick gets ~850 of those reads. At **one tick per day** (`0 5 * * *`), planning that sweep takes about six daily ticks before a single delete lands.

And the growth makes it marginal rather than merely slow: inventory has been climbing ~750 narinfos/day, so roughly as many paths cross grace each day as one tick can collect. The collector is close to never converging.

What I can't determine from outside: whether that tick **froze** or **threw**. Both look identical through the API — no report. Separating them needs the worker's logs (a `gc.paused` event vs an exception) or a read of `meta/gc-cursor`, and both need the Cloudflare account token, which I don't have here. If you can pull up the worker's observability for 8 Sep 05:00, that settles it in one look.

The cheap fix is the cron. Runs are already resumable and idempotent across ticks, so `0 * * * *` gives 24 ticks a day instead of 1 and the current backlog drains in hours instead of a week. It's one line — `GC_CRON` at `infra/alchemy.run.ts:20`, which feeds both the binding and `crons` — but it's a production deploy, so I'm not touching it without your say. The deeper fix is removing the per-candidate narinfo read from the collect stage, which is a real design change rather than a one-liner.

Want me to start with the cron, or dig into the collect stage first?

Confirmed, with hard numbers from the collector's own artifacts. My freeze read was right; the account was the only thing I had wrong.

**The 8 Sep run is parked.** `meta/gc-cursor` in `cachet-production`:

```
run id     1788843694314-2a7a4177f346ec84   started 08 Sep 05:01:34 UTC
stage      candidates          (the collect stage)
inventory  14,634 narinfos / 38,242 objects
mark       complete — 300 visited, frontier empty
collect    534 collected
```

**And the earlier zeros were legitimate,** now proven rather than inferred. The 7 Sep run's own plan artifact reads `{"candidates":0,"narinfoDeletes":0,"narDeletes":0}` — genuinely nothing eligible. Grace, exactly as the table suggested. (`meta/generation` is at 2, bumped 22 Aug — that's the poison-sig hand-bump, not the collector.)

**The budget arithmetic checks out exactly.** Tick one spent: 1 cursor read + 39 list pages (38,242 objects at 1,000/page) + 2 artifact/lease ops + 300 mark reads + 534 collect reads + 1 cursor write = 877 of 900. That's why it stopped at 534. Later ticks skip the mark reads, so they get **~857 collect reads each**.

**It doesn't converge.** Today's eligible pool is the 25 Aug inventory crossing grace — ~4,900 paths. But the window keeps sliding, and the daily increments from the report table become eligible 14 days later: +1,139 on 9 Sep, +1,027 on 10 Sep, then a **+4,425 cliff on 14 Sep** and +2,330 on 17 Sep. Against 857 collected per tick, the backlog goes 4,432 → 4,714 → 4,884 → dips to ~2,500 by 13 Sep → back to 6,058 on 14 Sep. The collect stage has to cover *every* current candidate before it can plan, so it never gets there and nothing is ever deleted. One tick per day is simply too few; it needs the push rate to fall below ~857 paths/day to ever finish.

The fix is the cron. `0 * * * *` gives 24 ticks a day, ~20,500 collect reads, which clears the whole backlog in a single day and then never falls behind. One line — `GC_CRON` at `infra/alchemy.run.ts:20`, feeding both the binding and `crons`.

One consequence to decide before you do it, though: health calls a deployment `degraded` when the newest report is older than **two days**, hardcoded at `crates/cachet-worker/src/api.rs:276` rather than derived from the cron. With an hourly cron that constant is 48 periods instead of 2, so it stops detecting a schedule that isn't firing. It should be two cron periods computed from `CACHET_GC_CRON`. (Separately: staging is going to read `degraded` from tomorrow's 05:02 regardless, because a parked multi-tick run lands no report at all — arguably health should read the cursor too.)

So there are three things here: the cron frequency, the health staleness bound, and the per-candidate narinfo read that makes collect this expensive in the first place. The first is a one-line production deploy. Want me to do that now and file the other two, or fix the health bound in the same commit so the cron change doesn't blind it?

content.text:
Your cache is never going to delete anything, and it's because the collector only gets to run once a day.

Here's the shape of it. The collector won't touch a path until it's been sitting unused for 14 days. Nothing in production was that old until this morning, which is why every run so far deleted zero. That part was fine and working as designed.

This morning about 4,900 paths finally aged past the 14 days. But before the collector can delete a path, it has to open that path's little metadata file to learn which data blob it points at, so it knows what to delete alongside it. That's one read per path. The worker gets a fixed work allowance per wake-up, roughly 900 operations, and it wakes up exactly once a day at 05:00. So this morning it got through 534 of the 4,900, wrote down where it stopped, and went back to sleep until tomorrow.

The trap is that it has to finish the entire list before it deletes anything at all. And every day that passes, another day's worth of paths crosses the 14-day line, because the window keeps sliding forward. You've been pushing roughly 1,100 paths a day, and the collector can only get through about 860 a day. So the finish line moves away from it faster than it walks toward it. It'll keep waking up, reading a few hundred more, and never actually reaching the end. Nothing gets deleted, the cache keeps growing, and you keep paying R2 for it.

The fix is to let it wake up every hour instead of once a day. Same allowance per wake-up, 24 times as many wake-ups, so it clears the whole backlog in about a day and then stays comfortably ahead. It's one line in the deploy config, and the runs already save their place and resume safely, so running more often is free of risk.

The one thing to sort out alongside it: the console's healthy/degraded light decides something is wrong if it hasn't seen a finished run in two days. That number is hardcoded rather than derived from how often the collector actually runs, so if we switch to hourly, that light stops being able to tell you the schedule has died. Worth fixing in the same change.

cat > docs/adr/0019-the-collector-fires-hourly.md <<'MDEOF'
# ADR 0019: The collector fires hourly, and health measures against that

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-09-08
- **Context doc:** [0005-gc-on-the-cron.md](0005-gc-on-the-cron.md);
  [../DEPLOY.md](../DEPLOY.md)

## Context

ADR 0005 gave the collector one firing a day and a per-invocation budget
of 900 binding operations, with runs that park a cursor and resume on the
next firing. Those two decisions interact in a way the original record
did not work through.

Before the sweep can delete a candidate's NAR, the collect stage has to
learn which NAR the candidate's narinfo names, and that is one bucket
read per candidate. A run plans nothing until it has collected every
candidate, so the reads a deployment can afford per day have to exceed
the paths that cross the grace window per day. One firing a day meant
about 860 reads after the listing and the mark stage took their share.

Production crossed that line on 8 September 2026, the first day anything
was old enough to sweep. The 14-day window expired on roughly 4,900
paths at once. The run collected 534 of them, parked, and waited for the
next day, while another day's worth of paths kept crossing the window at
over a thousand a day. The candidate set was growing faster than the
collector could read it, so no run would ever reach its sweep. Fourteen
runs had already deleted nothing, and the inventory had gone from 4,966
narinfos to 14,634.

The health route had a related problem, invisible until the schedule
changed. Its staleness bound was two days, written as a constant rather
than derived from the cron, so it happened to mean two cron periods
only while the cron was daily.

## Decision

1. The cron is `0 * * * *`. Twenty-four firings a day multiply the
   collect stage's daily allowance by twenty-four and change no single
   invocation's ceiling, so nothing about the per-run budget, the
   resumability, or the gates moves.
2. Health's staleness bound is two of the deployment's own cron periods,
   read from `CACHET_GC_CRON` through the schedule parser. A cron the
   parser does not recognize falls back to two days, which is the loose
   answer rather than one guessed from an expression nobody read.
3. The schedule parser recognizes the hourly shape (`M * * * *`) beside
   the daily one (`M H * * *`) and reports the period of each. Every
   other cron expression still answers nothing, so a console shows no
   countdown rather than a wrong one.
4. Health reads `meta/gc-cursor` and treats a parked run as proof the
   schedule fired. Reports land only when a run concludes, so a
   collection spanning many ticks leaves the newest report aging while
   the collector works, and with an hourly bound that would answer
   `degraded` during ordinary operation.

## Consequences

A deployment collects on the hour. A tick with nothing to do spends its
listing and exits, so the added firings cost a bucket listing an hour on
an idle cache. Production's 4,900-path backlog drains in about six
firings instead of never.

The colour on the console now means something on both schedules: an
hourly deployment goes `degraded` after two missed hours, where it used
to need two days of silence, which is forty-eight missed firings.

Health costs one more bucket read per request. It is an admin route the
console polls, and the read is a `get` on one small key.

## Alternatives considered

**Raise `GC_OP_BUDGET`.** More reads per firing rather than more
firings. Rejected: the budget exists to keep one invocation inside the
platform's subrequest and CPU ceilings, and raising it trades a
collector that cannot finish for invocations that get killed partway.

**Bound the collect stage instead: plan and sweep what has been
collected so far.** This converges without touching the cron, and it is
the more thorough fix, because it removes the requirement that one run
see every candidate. Rejected for now: partial plans mean a NAR whose
narinfo was collected in one run and swept in another, and working out
which orderings stay safe is a larger change than the schedule that was
starving it. Worth doing if the read per candidate ever becomes the
bottleneck again.

**Store each narinfo's NAR key beside it at write time** so the collect
stage needs no read at all. The measurement written when a NAR lands
(ADR 0012) is the natural place. This is the real fix to the cost and
not just to the allowance, and it stays open.
MDEOF

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSGEOF'
The collector fires hourly, so it can outpace its own backlog

Production's collector could not finish a run. Before the sweep deletes a
candidate's NAR, the collect stage reads that candidate's narinfo to learn
which NAR it names, one bucket read each, and a run plans nothing until it
has collected every candidate. Against a 900-operation budget and one
firing a day, that left about 860 reads a day while paths crossed the
14-day grace window at over a thousand a day. On 8 September the first
4,900 paths aged out at once, the run collected 534 and parked, and the
candidate set was growing faster than the reads could cover it. Fourteen
runs had deleted nothing and the inventory had gone from 4,966 narinfos to
14,634.

The cron is now `0 * * * *`. Twenty-four firings multiply the daily
allowance by twenty-four and change no single invocation's ceiling, so the
per-run budget, the resumability, and the gates all stand as they were. A
tick with nothing to collect spends its listing and exits.

Health had to change with it. Its staleness bound was two days written as
a constant, which meant two cron periods only while the cron was daily;
across an hourly one it is forty-eight firings, and a colour that needs
two days of silence reports nothing. The bound now comes from the
deployment's own cron, so the schedule parser recognizes the hourly shape
beside the daily one and reports each period. An expression it does not
recognize keeps the two-day fallback.

Health also reads the cursor now. Reports land only when a run concludes,
so a collection spanning many ticks leaves the newest report aging while
the collector works, and against an hourly bound that would answer
degraded during ordinary operation. A parked cursor is proof the schedule
fired.

The workerd lane covers the staleness bound in both directions from one
seed, and its own cron is the shipped shape. ADR 0019 records it; 0005
and 0013 are amended, and the ADR index gets the rows 0014 through 0018
never got.
MSGEOF
git log --oneline -1; git cat-file commit HEAD | grep -c gpgsig

content.text:
Done and pushed as `912e5b0`. CI is running, and I'm watching it plus the staging deploy that follows.

What went in:

**The cron is hourly.** `GC_CRON` at `infra/alchemy.run.ts:20` is now `0 * * * *`, feeding both the platform trigger and the worker's own copy so the countdown can't disagree with what fires. Nothing about the per-invocation budget, the cursor, or the gates moved — there are just 24 times as many invocations per day.

**Health measures against that cron instead of a constant.** The staleness bound was a hardcoded two days, which only happened to mean two cron periods while the cron was daily. It now comes from the deployment's own `CACHET_GC_CRON`, so the schedule parser learned the hourly shape (`M * * * *`) alongside the daily one and reports each period. An expression it doesn't recognise keeps the two-day fallback rather than a bound guessed from something nobody parsed.

**Health also reads the cursor.** This is the part that would have bitten us on deploy: reports only land when a run *concludes*, so production's ~6-hour backlog drain would have left the newest report aging with no new one behind it, and an hourly bound would have painted `degraded` through the whole recovery. A parked cursor is proof the schedule fired, so it now reads healthy while a run is in flight.

Gates: unit 219, golden, property, console 51, workerd 106 (including two new rows — a parked cursor keeps an aging report healthy, and deleting that cursor makes the same report read degraded, both from one seed via a new `r2Delete` driver helper), clippy on both targets, openapi drift, and both manifest bijections. ADR 0019 records the decision, 0005 and 0013 are amended, and I added the ADR index rows for 0014 through 0018 that I'd never written.

Two things to flag:

The first commit attempt failed with `1Password: failed to fill whole buffer` and wrote nothing. The retry signed fine, and `912e5b0` carries its signature — I didn't touch the signing setup.

Production won't pick this up from this push. Staging deploys off green main; production only moves on a tag. So production is still on `v0.1.2` with the daily cron and that parked run from 05:01 this morning, which means it'll fire once more at 05:00 tomorrow and collect another ~860. Want me to cut `v0.1.3` once staging is verified, or hold?

lastPrompt: bruh. Okay. Do it.

The hourly cron works, proven end to end on a real deployment.

Staging fired at **01:00:46 UTC** and finished six seconds later, having swept the one dead path in its bucket: 1 narinfo, 1 NAR, 575 bytes freed, no gate. Its previous run was 8 Sep 05:01, so this is the first firing on the new schedule and it landed on the hour.

That also exercises the whole chain in production conditions: alchemy pushed the new trigger, the platform accepted it, the worker's own `CACHET_GC_CRON` matches what fires, and a run with an empty candidate set costs almost nothing.

So the state of things:

- `912e5b0` — hourly cron, health measured against it, cursor read
- `0cb6f6a` — the yanked `chacha20` bump
- CI green on all 16, staging deployed, integration lane green, hourly collection observed firing

Correcting one thing I said a few minutes ago: I reported "still nothing several minutes past the hour", which was wrong. My polling loop had a baseline timestamp three days in the future, so it could never have fired. The deployment was fine the whole time.

Production is the one thing left. It's on `v0.1.2` with the daily cron and a parked run, so at 05:00 UTC it takes one more tick of ~860 candidates and parks again. A tag is the only thing that moves it, and that's yours to call.
