# CLAUDE.md: the deployer constitution

The deployer installs nox products into customers' own Cloudflare accounts
and keeps them updated there. It is written in Rust with workers-rs and a
React client. This document binds every contribution and every agent that
works in this repository. Every rule carries its reason.

## §0 The prime directive

A gate, lane, or doc name exists in conversation only when it exists in the
flake, the justfile, or the manifest. Suggesting a check that cannot run is
a defect. When you add one, land the verb, the CI job, and the doc row in
one commit.

## §1 The stack

Four programs and a contract. The contract is the product manifest
(docs/product-manifest.md): a product's CI emits it, signs it, and publishes
it with content-addressed blobs. The control plane is a workers-rs worker
with three Durable Object classes, KV for sessions, and R2 for releases; it
holds identity, desired state, and the event log, and it serves the client
as static assets. The agent is a workers-rs worker installed into each
customer's account under an account-owned token; it reads desired state,
verifies releases, applies them with the engine, and reports every step.
The engine is a pure crate both workers and a product's own CLI share. The
client is a React application in `web/`. Cloudflare's OAuth is the only
identity; an operation inside an account runs under an access token the
person granted minutes before, and nothing is ever refreshed.

## §2 The prose law

PROSE.md governs every Markdown file, comment, and user-visible string in
this repository, including its own README. The doc-manifest gate enforces
that the manifest in §11 loads all of it.

## §3 Clock, entropy, and layout determinism

Time is sampled where a decision needs it and passed down; entropy enters
only in the control plane's `rand` module and the browser's key
generation; map layout uses BTreeMap and BTreeSet. clippy.toml bans the
ambient forms and the ban is mechanical, not advisory. Banned verbatim:
SystemTime::now, Instant::now, thread::spawn, HashMap, HashSet.

## §4 Crate boundaries

The dependency direction is one-way. deployer-manifest is pure and knows
no product; deployer-engine is pure and knows no runtime; deployer-api
describes the HTTP surfaces and generates the OpenAPI document;
deployer-cloudflare is the engine's trait over workers-rs fetch;
deployer-agent and deployer-control are the wasm32 deployables that own
every binding; `web/` depends on the HTTP surface and on nothing in the
workspace. The three wasm32 crates are excluded from workspace
default-members and from the host gates; their build and their truth lane
are the wasm verbs. A path dependency against this direction fails review.

## §5 Wasm and crypto hygiene

ring, aws-lc-rs, aws-lc-sys, and openssl-sys are banned outright in
deny.toml, because nothing here builds for a host that needs TLS. Hashing
uses sha2, signing uses ed25519-dalek, and grants and releases carry
ed25519 signatures. scripts/check-wasm-hygiene.sh scans both shipped
bundles for the banned runtimes and for secret-shaped strings; the gate
protects the artifact, not intentions. Only the worker crates enable
getrandom's js backend, so library crates stay honest about owning no
entropy.

## §6 Dependencies

Versions pin exactly where generation behavior matters and by minor series
elsewhere. New dependencies need one `// why:` comment at their
Cargo.toml entry: what they do and why nothing in the tree already does it.

## §7 Errors and panics

External-input failures are typed errors with the error table's vocabulary
(deployer-api's ErrorCode); RFC 9457 problem+json bodies leave both
workers. Invariant violations panic with named invariants, and an
attacker-reachable condition never panics. Test code panics on missing
fixtures rather than skipping. No event, error, or log line carries a
secret's value, a grant, a token, or a session id.

## §8 The manifest gates

Four bijections keep docs and runs honest, all enforced by scripts in
`scripts/`: the §11 manifest against the repo's non-ADR Markdown
(check-doc-manifest.sh), docs/testing/lanes.toml against the lane docs
and CI jobs (check-lane-manifest.sh), deployer-api's route descriptors
against the committed docs/openapi.yaml (check-openapi-drift.sh), and the
agent's roster against the committed
fixtures/deployer-agent/deploy-manifest.json (check-agent-manifest.sh).

## §9 The lanes

Every test belongs to exactly one lane, and each lane is job-named the
same everywhere: the lanes.toml row, the docs/testing doc, the just verb,
and the CI job. A failed test that passes on retry is a bug, never a flake:
retries stay zero. The registry docs/testing/lanes.toml is the list.

## §10 Comments

Code comments state why, not what: `// why:` begins every non-obvious
choice so the reason greps. Rustdoc states what a public item does; the
comment beside it states why the code chose this way.

## §11 Required context

The manifest below is the bijection's source. Scripts assert it loads
exactly the repo's non-ADR Markdown, no more and no less.

@README.md
@PROSE.md
@SECURITY.md
@docs/product-manifest.md
@docs/operating.md
@docs/client.md
@docs/security/threat-model.md
@docs/testing/unit.md
@docs/testing/property.md
@docs/testing/golden.md
@docs/testing/client.md
@docs/testing/workerd.md
EOF
cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# deployer

The deployer installs nox products into your own Cloudflare account and
keeps them updated there. You sign in with Cloudflare, pick a product and
an account, answer the product's questions, and an agent the deployer
installs into your account creates the product's resources, applies its
signed release, and reports each step back to the page you are watching.
Updates, configuration changes, secret rotations, and uninstalls go the
same way. cachet is the first product; sesame is next.

The repo holds the product manifest contract, the engine that renders and
applies manifests, the two workers, the client, and the lanes that prove
them.

## For people installing a product

Open the deployer, choose "Continue with Cloudflare", and follow the
wizard. It asks for a name and an address, the product's configuration,
and the product's secrets, and it authorizes one operation in your
account along the way. What the agent can and cannot do in your account is
written in [docs/security/threat-model.md](docs/security/threat-model.md).
The client is described in [docs/client.md](docs/client.md).

## For people publishing a product

A product publishes a manifest and content-addressed blobs to the
deployer's release store and signs the manifest with its release key. The
contract is [docs/product-manifest.md](docs/product-manifest.md); the
store layout and the promotion marker are in
[docs/operating.md](docs/operating.md).

## For people running the deployer

The control plane deploys with wrangler from
`crates/deployer-control/wrangler.toml`; its bindings, secrets, the
Cloudflare OAuth client it needs, and the release keys it trusts are in
[docs/operating.md](docs/operating.md).

## Repository layout

- `crates/`: the workspace. `deployer-manifest` (the contract),
  `deployer-engine` (render and apply), `deployer-api` (the HTTP surfaces
  and the generated OpenAPI document), `deployer-cloudflare` (the
  Cloudflare API over workers-rs fetch), `deployer-agent` and
  `deployer-control` (the two wasm32 deployables).
- `web/`: the client the control plane serves.
- `fixtures/`: each product's committed manifest template, and the agent's.
- `docs/`: product-manifest.md (the contract), operating.md (running the
  service and publishing releases), client.md (the client),
  security/threat-model.md, testing/ (the lanes), adr/ (decision records),
  openapi.yaml (generated, drift-gated).
- `workerd/`: the workerd lane's driver and both workers' lane configs.

## Governing documents

| Document | Role |
| --- | --- |
| [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) | The constitution: invariants, lanes, and the doc manifest. |
| [PROSE.md](PROSE.md) | The prose law every repo document obeys. |
| [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) | The vulnerability disclosure policy. |

## License

Apache-2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).
EOF
cat > SECURITY.md <<'EOF'
# Security policy

Report vulnerabilities through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting for
this repository. Do not open public issues for suspected vulnerabilities.

## Scope

The security model covers the hosted components: the control plane, the
agent the deployer installs into a customer's account, the client, and the
release store. A customer's Cloudflare account, the products installed into
it, and the secrets they type belong to the customer and are out of scope
for reports about the deployer itself, except where the deployer handles
them: a grant that admits a value it should not, a control plane that can
read a secret, or a release that installs without a valid signature is in
scope.

The threat model in docs/security/threat-model.md describes the attacker
scenarios the deployer defends against and the mechanisms and tests that
enforce each defense. A report that breaks one of those mechanisms with a
reproduction is always in scope.

## Supported versions

The deployer is pre-1.0 and the main branch is the only supported version.
Fixes land on main and ship in the next tagged release.

## Expectations

Reports get an acknowledgement within a week. Fixes ship before disclosure,
and disclosure happens with credit, unless you ask otherwise.
EOF
mkdir -p docs/security docs/testing docs/adr && cat > docs/security/threat-model.md <<'EOF'
# Threat model

The deployer acts inside other people's Cloudflare accounts, so the model
starts from the placement that matters most: what an attacker holding each
part of the system can and cannot do in a customer's account. Every
scenario names the defense in force and where it is proven. A customer's
own account hygiene, their Cloudflare credentials, and the products they
install are outside this document's scope.

## What is protected

A customer's secrets: the values they type or the browser generates, which
the deployer must never be able to read. A customer's account: nothing the
deployer does there may exceed what the person authorized for that
operation, and nothing may stay behind that they did not choose to keep.
The releases: what an agent installs must be what a product's CI signed.
The identity: a session must be the person who signed in with Cloudflare,
and an agent must be the one the control plane installed.

## The trust boundary

The control plane can set a product's vars, choose among signed releases,
ask an agent to reconcile or to tear down, and issue grants. It cannot read
any secret, install code nobody signed, delete a bucket, or act in an
account outside an operation the person authorized minutes before. The
agent trusts two signatures: the control plane's key on grants and the
product's release key on manifests. It trusts nothing unsigned, and it
holds a secret only from the browser's post to the upload that carries it.

## Scenarios

**A compromised control plane.** An attacker runs the control plane's
code or reads its storage. What they find: instance records, desired
state, event logs, session ids, agent key hashes, and for the minutes of
an operation an access token for one account. What they can do: change a
product's configuration, move an instance to another published release, and
ask for a teardown of the worker and namespace. What they cannot do: read a
secret (none passes through the control plane; the client posts them to
the agent under a grant, and the agent's `/secrets` route verifies the
grant and stores the values in the agent's own storage), install code
(the agent verifies each manifest's signature under the product's release
keys before it reads the manifest, and the control plane holds no release
key's secret half), or delete a bucket (the agent deletes one only after a
delete-bucket grant arrives with the instance's name typed, from the
browser). Proven: the workerd lane's rows that post a secret and assert it
appears in the stub account and in neither the control plane's log nor its
event log, that a forged grant is refused, that a bucket survives a
teardown until the name is typed, and the manifest crate's signature tests.

**A compromised agent token.** The account-owned token an agent runs under
leaks. Its policies are the product's: Workers Scripts, KV, R2, and
Hyperdrive on the account, and Zone Read, DNS, and Workers Routes on the
custom domain's zone. It can rewrite the product's worker and read the
bucket. It cannot read the customer's other zones, mint tokens, or act on
the deployer. The customer revokes it in the dashboard; uninstalling
revokes it through the API. Proven: the lane asserts the token's request
carries exactly an account policy and, for a custom domain, one zone
policy, and that uninstalling deletes the token.

**A replayed or forged grant.** An attacker replays a captured grant or
signs one with another key. A grant is an ed25519 signature by the control
plane over claims naming the instance, the purpose, the secret names, a
nonce, and an expiry ten minutes out; the agent verifies it under the
control plane's public key, refuses another instance's, another purpose's,
or an expired one, and refuses a body naming a secret outside the grant.
Replay within the window sets the same names again, which the agent then
re-applies; a replay cannot set a name the grant did not carry. Proven: the
grant module's tests and the lane's forged-grant and out-of-grant rows.

**A tampered release.** An attacker with write access to the release
store changes a manifest or a blob. The manifest's signature no longer
verifies and the agent refuses it before parsing; a blob whose bytes do
not hash to the name the manifest recorded is refused before upload.
Proven: the signature tests, the engine's tampered-blob test, and the
lane's signed publication.

**A stolen session.** A session cookie leaves a browser. It is HttpOnly,
Secure, SameSite=Lax, a random id in KV with a fourteen-day expiry, and it
carries no Cloudflare credential: every operation in an account still
needs the person's fresh consent on Cloudflare's own page, so a session
alone can read records and change configuration but cannot act in the
account. Logout deletes the KV record. Proven: the lane's cookie
attributes, replayed-state refusal, and the 428 an operation answers
without an authorization.

**A held authorization outliving its operation.** The access token an
operation runs under is held on the user's object until it expires or the
operation ends. A provisioning deletes it when it answers; a teardown holds
its copy on the instance object until the agent reports the worker gone,
then removes the agent and revokes the token; an alarm drops either at
expiry. No refresh token exists because `offline_access` is never asked
for. Proven: the lane asserts the zone listing answers 428 again after
provisioning, and that the operation's token is revoked at the end of a
teardown.

**Name collisions in the account.** The account already holds a worker
under the name an install would use. Every worker the engine uploads
carries ownership tags, and pre-flight reads them: absent, this instance's,
another instance's, a newer deployer's, or not deployed here. Only the
first two proceed. Proven: the engine's pre-flight tests and the lane's
name check.

**Secrets in logs or artifacts.** Both workers log JSON events with step
names, versions, and reasons and never values; the wasm-hygiene gate scans
both bundles for secret-shaped strings; the property lane asserts over
arbitrary secret values that no plan, no kept render, and no event carries
one. Proven: `just wasm-hygiene`, the property lane, and the lane's log
assertions.

**Supply chain of the deployer itself.** cargo deny bans ring, aws-lc,
and openssl outright, exact pins hold utoipa and hegel, and the hygiene
scan refuses banned symbols in the artifacts. Proven: `just deny`,
`just wasm-hygiene`.

## Non-goals

No defense against a customer's own Cloudflare account takeover: the
account's own authentication governs that, and an attacker holding it holds
everything the deployer could do there and more. No rate limiting beyond
the platform's. No defense against a product whose own code misuses the
bindings it is given; the manifest declares what a product gets, and the
product's own threat model governs what it does with it.
EOF
cat > docs/product-manifest.md <<'EOF'
# The product manifest

A product manifest is the contract between a product's CI and the
deployer. It describes one release of one product as a template: every
account-specific value is a placeholder from a closed set, and the
deployer renders the placeholders from an instance's own state before it
touches an account. The deployer knows no product; each product emits its
manifest from its own repository and the deployer reads the shape.

## The shape

A manifest is a JSON document with `manifestVersion` 1 and these parts:

| Part | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `product`, `version` | Identity. `product` is also the prefix every resource carries. |
| `worker` | `mainModule`, `modules[{name, kind}]`, `compatibilityDate`, `compatibilityFlags`, `observability`, `limits.cpuMs`, and `migrations.newSqliteClasses` for a worker with Durable Objects. |
| `resources[]` | What an install creates, each with a `key` bindings reference: `r2_bucket {name}`, `kv_namespace {title}`, `analytics_engine {dataset}`, `hyperdrive {name, origin}`, `d1 {name}`, `queue {name}`. Names are templates. |
| `bindings[]` | `{type, name, resource}`, or `{type: assets}`, `{type: send_email}`, `{type: durable_object_namespace, className}`. |
| `vars[]` | `{name, requirement, value, env, default, summary, wizard}`. `requirement` is `required`, `optional`, or `derived`. |
| `secrets[]` | `{name, requirement, value, env, summary, wizard, generated}`. |
| `crons[]` | `{expression, var}`: the trigger, and the var that must carry the same expression when one does. |
| `route` | `customDomain` (`required`, `optional`, `none`), `workersDev`, `hostIsIdentity`. |
| `assets` | `{directory, base, htmlHandling, notFoundHandling}`, for a product that serves files. |
| `verify[]` | Probes run after an apply: `{get, status}` or `{get, jsonPath, equals}`. |
| `console` | `{path}`, for the deep link. |
| `artifacts` | `{modules[{name, sha256, size}], assets{path: {hash, size}}}`. Absent on the committed template; the release workflow fills it. |

The wizard hints on a var or secret are `label`, `help`, `consoleUrl`,
`setupSteps[]`, and `redirectUriTemplate`, and the client renders each
question from them. A secret with `generated: {kind: ed25519NixKey,
keyName, previousKeysVar}` is made in the browser rather than asked for;
`previousKeysVar` names the var that lists earlier public halves after a
rotation, when the product has one.

## The placeholders

The set is closed. A `$` followed by an uppercase letter must begin one of
these or the manifest is refused:

| Token | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `$NAME` | the instance's name as the operator wrote it |
| `$RESOURCE_NAME` | the name every account resource is created under |
| `$RESOURCE_NAME_UNDERSCORED` | the same with dashes as underscores |
| `$HOST` | the instance's host |
| `$VERSION` | the release's version |
| `$VAR(<binding>)` | the operator's value for a var |
| `$SECRET(<binding>)` | the operator's value for a secret |
| `$GENERATED_PUBLIC(<secret>)` | the public half of a key the browser generated |

A `$` followed by anything else is a literal, so a JSON path like
`$.version` in a probe passes through. A `$SECRET` may appear only in a
secret's value and in a Hyperdrive origin; a var, a resource name, a probe
expectation, or a key name that names one is refused, because those places
are printed.

A var whose template names no `$VAR` renders from the instance alone. A
host var written `$HOST` is such a var: the wizard's address step answers
it, and the engine never asks for a value of its own.

## Names

An instance name is a lowercase word of 2 to 32 characters: a letter, then
letters, digits, and dashes. Every resource is created under
`<product>-<name>`, or the name as it is when it already carries the
prefix, so no customer reads `cachet-cachet-*` in their account. The agent
installed for a product's instance is named `<product>-deployment-<name>`.

## Publication

A release is published to the deployer's R2 bucket in this order: every
module and asset under `blobs/<hash>` (a module's SHA-256 hex, an asset's
32-character hash), then `releases/<product>/<version>/manifest.json` with
`artifacts` filled in, then `releases/<product>/<version>/manifest.sig`,
the base64 ed25519 signature over the manifest's bytes as published.
Promoting a release writes its version into
`releases/<product>/promoted`. A new install takes the promoted release;
an instance with automatic updates moves to it after its delay.

The agent verifies the signature under the product's release keys before
it parses the manifest, and verifies every module's hash before it
uploads. The control plane carries each product's public keys in
`RELEASE_KEYS_JSON` and passes them into each agent it installs.

## Validation

`Manifest::from_json` in deployer-manifest refuses another schema version,
a binding naming a resource nothing declares, a duplicate key or name, an
entry module missing from the module list, a cron whose var disagrees, a
template that does not parse, a secret in a printable place, a secret whose
value is not a secret template, and artifacts that do not cover the
modules exactly. cachet's committed manifest is a fixture here, and the
golden lane asserts it reads back to the bytes cachet wrote.
EOF
cat > docs/operating.md <<'EOF'
# Operating the deployer

This document is for the people who run the control plane and for the
products that publish to it. The customer's side is docs/client.md.

## The control plane's bindings

The control plane deploys with wrangler from
`crates/deployer-control/wrangler.toml`. It binds one KV namespace
(`SESSIONS`, holding sessions and OAuth states), one R2 bucket (`RELEASES`,
the release store), three Durable Object classes (`USERS`, `INSTANCES`,
`RELEASE_INDEX`), and the client's built files as `ASSETS`. Its vars and
secrets:

| Binding | Kind | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PUBLIC_URL` | var | The deployment's own origin, in every URL it hands out. |
| `OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` | var | The Cloudflare OAuth client. |
| `OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` | secret | Its secret. |
| `OAUTH_IDENTITY_SCOPES` | var | The scopes a sign-in asks for; default `user-details.read account-settings.read`. |
| `OAUTH_WRITE_SCOPES` | var | The scopes an operation asks for. The default names the Workers, KV, R2, Zone, DNS, and account-token scopes; verify them against `GET /oauth/scopes` when the client is made and set this var if they differ. |
| `CONTROL_SIGNING_SEED` | secret | 32 random bytes, base64: the ed25519 seed grants are signed with. Its public half goes into every agent. |
| `RELEASE_KEYS_JSON` | var | `{"cachet": ["<base64 public key>"], "deployer-agent": ["..."]}`: the release keys each product's manifests must be signed under. The agent is a product here too. |
| `AGENT_TOKEN_PERMISSIONS_JSON` | var | Optional. The permission group names an agent's token carries on the account and on the zone; unset takes the defaults in `settings.rs`. |
| `CF_OAUTH_BASE_URL`, `CF_API_BASE_URL` | var | Lane only: the stub's addresses. Unset takes Cloudflare's. |
| `AGENT_URL_OVERRIDE`, `PRODUCT_PROBE_BASE_OVERRIDE` | var | Lane only: where the agent and the product's probes are, instead of their workers.dev and custom-domain hosts. |

## The OAuth client

Create a Cloudflare OAuth client for the deployment with redirect URI
`<PUBLIC_URL>/v1/auth/callback` and authorization code with PKCE. The
deployer never asks for `offline_access`: a sign-in yields a session and
the identity token is revoked; an operation yields an access token that is
held for at most the token's lifetime and never refreshed.

## What an operation authorizes

Deploying and uninstalling act inside the customer's account, so each asks
the person to authorize the account on Cloudflare's consent page. The
authorization is held on the user's record until it expires or the
operation ends. Provisioning reads the account's workers.dev subdomain,
mints the agent's account-owned token with the permission groups in
`AGENT_TOKEN_PERMISSIONS_JSON`, uploads the agent, and discards the
authorization. Uninstalling holds its copy on the instance until the agent
reports the worker gone, then removes the agent, deletes its token, and
revokes the authorization.

## Publishing a product

A product's release workflow builds its worker and assets, emits its
manifest, measures every module and asset into `artifacts`, signs the
manifest with the product's release key, and uploads to the release store
in the order docs/product-manifest.md gives: blobs, manifest, signature.
Writing the version into `releases/<product>/promoted` promotes it; new
installs and automatic updates follow the promotion. The public half of the
release key goes into `RELEASE_KEYS_JSON`; rotating the key means adding the
new half beside the old until every release signed under the old one has
aged out.

The agent publishes the same way. `just agent-manifest` regenerates its
template from its roster in deployer-api; the release workflow measures the
bundle `just wasm` built into it and publishes it under `deployer-agent`.
An agent updates itself when the promoted agent release differs from the
version it runs, once per promoted version.

## Automatic updates

An instance with automatic updates on looks at the index hourly and moves
to the promoted release once it has been promoted for the instance's delay,
so a customer's own staging instance meets a release before their
production one does. The choice of version is the control plane's; the
applying is the agent's, in the account. "Hold" pins an instance whatever
is promoted.

## Deploying the control plane

`just web` builds the client, `just wasm` builds both bundles, and
`wrangler deploy --config crates/deployer-control/wrangler.toml` deploys
the control plane with the client as its assets. The `deploy` workflow does
the same from a tag, with the vars and secrets above as environment
secrets. The agent is not deployed by wrangler: the control plane installs
the promoted agent release into each customer's account.

## Running a product's install from a terminal

The engine is a plain crate. A product's CLI can depend on it and run the
same plan, converge, and uninstall against the real API with a token the
operator supplies, which is how cachet's `cachet deploy` works without
this service.
EOF
cat > docs/client.md <<'EOF'
# The client

The control plane serves a browser client at its root. It is the cachet
console's sibling: the same tokens, the same primitives, the same rule that
screens carry facts and this document carries explanations. Where the
console has no inputs, the client is mostly inputs, and this document says
what each one does.

## The screens

**Sign in** is one button, "Continue with Cloudflare", and three plain
statements: you approve access on the Cloudflare dashboard; a small agent
is installed in your account that creates the product's resources there,
applies signed releases, and reports what it did; the code is open source
and the same install runs from the command line. It names the threat model
for what the agent can and cannot do.

**Instances** is the home: one row per instance across every connected
account, with product and name, host, account, installed and desired
version, and status. An empty list says what an instance is and offers
"New instance".

**New instance** asks one question per screen, with a rail that fills in
as answers arrive. The steps, in order: product and account; authorize;
name and address; configuration; secrets; options; deploy. The
authorization is the second step because it is a full-page redirect
through Cloudflare's consent, and a secret must never have to survive one:
the draft that does survive it (product, account, name, address, vars,
options) is kept in the browser's session storage, and secrets are typed
afterwards and kept in memory only. The name is checked live against the
grammar and, once authorized, against the account. The address is a custom
domain in one of the account's zones or workers.dev, as the product's
manifest allows; when the host is the product's identity, the step says
that moving it later is a key rotation. Configuration renders each
required var from the manifest's wizard hints, with setup steps, the
console page, and the redirect URI filled in. Secrets generates the keys
the manifest says to generate, in the browser, and requires the secret
half to be downloaded before continuing; typed secrets are entered once.
Options holds every var with a default and the update policy. Deploy
creates the record, provisions the agent under the authorization, posts
the secrets to the agent under the grant provisioning answered, and opens
the instance page.

**Instance** shows the facts (product, name, host, account, versions,
status) and five tabs. Overview shows the latest operation's steps live
from the event stream and the operation list. Configuration edits vars
and previews the change before applying it. Secrets replaces a typed
secret or rotates a generated key: the new key is generated in the
browser, downloaded, posted to the agent under a grant, and its public
half recorded, with the old public half appended to the var the manifest
names for previous keys when it names one. Updates shows installed,
desired, and promoted, the release list, and the update policy; an update
previews the binding diff and collects any secret the target release adds.
Uninstall lists by name what goes, offers to keep or delete the bucket,
requires the instance's name typed back, and needs a fresh authorization,
because removing the agent and its token is the control plane's own work
in the account.

**Account** lists the connected accounts and offers to connect another,
which is another sign-in.

## The event stream

Every operation's steps arrive over a WebSocket per instance, resumed by
sequence number, so a refresh mid-operation shows the same list a patient
tab shows. The page is read once over HTTP first, so a browser whose
WebSocket is blocked still reads the log. A step row is a dot, the step,
its detail, and its elapsed time; a failed row grows its remedy.

## The signal colour

The console paints a healthy status and a refusal the same red. A deploy
flow has many success states, and a step list where done is red reads as
failure, so the client uses the signal colour for a failed step, a refused
input, and an armed destructive button, and for nothing that succeeded.
Text is done, muted is pending, amber is running or waiting on something
outside the account.

## How it is built and served

React with TanStack Router and Query, StyleX against the console's tokens,
and `effect` schemas at every wire boundary: a control plane newer or older
than the client beside it fails at the boundary with the field named. Keys
are generated with WebCrypto's Ed25519 and written in nix's own format,
which is what cachet's worker parses and a laptop's nix trusts. `just web`
builds into `web/dist`, which the control plane serves as its assets. Its
tests are the client lane (docs/testing/client.md).
EOF
cat > docs/testing/lanes.toml <<'EOF'
# The lane table (CLAUDE.md §9). One [lane.<id>] table per test lane. The id
# equals the CI job id, the just verb, and the living doc's basename in
# docs/testing/. A lane earns its row when its CI job runs: the row, the
# doc, and the job land in one commit. scripts/check-lane-manifest.sh
# asserts the bijection both ways.

[lane.unit]
summary = "Logic, parsing, and state-machine bugs in the pure crates, and the operations against the in-memory Cloudflare."

[lane.property]
summary = "Pure laws over arbitrary inputs: grammar totality, no secret value in any plan or render, round-trips."

[lane.golden]
summary = "The exact bytes of the wire contracts: cachet's manifest read back, the plan, the script metadata, the OpenAPI document."

[lane.client]
summary = "The client's pure derivations, its components, and the schemas it decodes every answer with."

[lane.workerd]
summary = "Both workers under workerd against a stub Cloudflare: sign-in, provisioning, secrets under grants, converge, reconfigure, rotate, teardown, asserted over real HTTP."
EOF
cat > docs/testing/unit.md <<'EOF'
# The unit lane

The unit lane runs `cargo nextest` over the workspace except the three
wasm32 crates, under the ci profile with zero retries
(`.config/nextest.toml`). It covers every pure function in
deployer-manifest, deployer-engine, and deployer-api: the placeholder
grammar, manifest validation, the plan and the render, the diff, grants,
the multipart bodies, the error table, and the agent's manifest template.
It also drives the engine's operations against the in-memory Cloudflare
(`deployer_engine::fake`): an install creates everything and a second run
creates nothing, pre-flight classifies every kind of collision, an update
keeps the secrets, a rotation uploads no code, and an uninstall keeps the
bucket unless told otherwise and empties it in pages when told.

A test in this lane is one concrete input with one asserted behavior.
Arbitrary-input coverage belongs to the property lane; byte-exact output
coverage belongs to the golden lane. A test that fails intermittently is a
determinism bug in the code or the test, and the fix is never a retry
(CLAUDE.md §9).

Run it: `just unit`.
EOF
cat > docs/testing/property.md <<'EOF'
# The property lane

The property lane runs one `tests/property.rs` per crate through hegel,
isolated from the unit lane so a property failure is its own signal. The
same cases also run inside the unit suite; the lane exists for the
standalone failure name.

Every crate with a property target states laws, not examples. The law
classes in force now:

- Totality. The placeholder grammar answers a parse or a typed refusal for
  any byte string, never a panic, and the name grammar answers for any
  string.
- No secret value anywhere printable. Over arbitrary secret values, a
  public render refuses a template naming a secret and its error names
  the binding and never the value; a plan and a kept-secrets render carry
  no secret's value; the one render that may carry them does.
- Round-trips. A manifest reads back from its own JSON to the same value
  and the same bytes, for the committed manifest and for perturbations of
  it.
- Determinism. The plan is a function of its arguments, and every name the
  grammar accepts derives a resource name the platform takes with the
  product prefix exactly once.

New classes join this list in the same commit as the code that obeys them.

Run it: `just property`.
EOF
cat > docs/testing/golden.md <<'EOF'
# The golden lane

The golden lane compares emitted bytes against committed expected bytes and
fails on drift, because every wire contract here is a byte-level fact: a
manifest a product signed as a file, metadata the Workers API parses, and
a plan a client shows.

The fixtures fall into two kinds. Cross-repository contracts are other
products' committed manifests: cachet's is read here and asserted to read
back to the bytes cachet wrote, which is what lets a manifest be signed as
a file and read as a document without the two ever disagreeing. Locked
shapes are authored here: the plan for cachet's manifest, the kept-secrets
script metadata, and the census of placeholders cachet uses.

Snapshots commit with the code that produces them. An intentional wire
change updates the snapshot in the same commit; the lane runs with
INSTA_UPDATE=no so CI can never quieten drift (CLAUDE.md §9). The served
OpenAPI document is the golden lane's served half: the workerd lane asserts
it byte-identical to docs/openapi.yaml.

Run it: `just golden`.
EOF
cat > docs/testing/client.md <<'EOF'
# The client lane

The client lane runs vitest over `web/`. It covers three kinds of code.

The pure derivations are everything between a decoded answer and a pixel:
which questions a manifest asks and in what order, what is still missing,
what the rail lists, how a flat event log becomes a step list, and the key
generation. The key test runs under node's WebCrypto and asserts the exact
nix format: the name, 88 characters of base64, 64 bytes, and a public half
equal to the last 32 of them.

The presentational components take props and no queries: the step list,
the field with its verdict, the pill, and the confirm dialog, whose
destructive button arms only once the name is typed back.

The schemas have their own file, and it is a drift check rather than a unit
test. Each case holds a body the control plane actually serializes, and
cachet's committed manifest is decoded through the manifest schema the
wizard reads. A field the control plane renames fails there, at the
boundary, rather than three components later as an `undefined` on screen.

What the lane does not do is drive the client against a control plane.
That is the workerd lane's job, where the driver is the browser.

Run it: `just client`. The build verb is separate: `just web` produces
`web/dist`, which the control plane serves.
EOF
cat > docs/testing/workerd.md <<'EOF'
# The workerd lane

The workerd lane runs both built bundles under `wrangler dev --local`,
which is miniflare over the real workerd binary: KV, R2, Durable Objects
with SQLite storage, WebSockets with hibernation, and the module pipeline
are the runtime's own. Assertions reach the workers over real HTTP from
`workerd/check.mjs`, a node script with no npm dependencies.

The driver runs a stub server that plays three roles: Cloudflare's API
(accounts, zones, permission groups, account tokens, the workers.dev
subdomain, script settings and multipart uploads, secrets, schedules,
domains, KV namespaces, R2 buckets and objects, asset upload sessions),
Cloudflare's OAuth server (a consent page that redirects straight back
with a code, a token endpoint that checks the PKCE challenge and the
client secret, and a revocation endpoint), and the customer's product host
as the verify probes see it. The stub parses every multipart upload and
keeps what the account would hold, so the assertions read the account's
state rather than a mock's call log.

The lane publishes two signed releases into the local release store before
booting anything: cachet at its committed manifest with stand-in modules,
and the agent at its committed manifest with the bundle `just wasm` built.
One release key signs both; a second key exists so a forged grant can be
refused on the record. The control plane boots first with the stub's
addresses and the two lane-only overrides that point every instance's
agent and probes at the lane's own processes. The driver then walks a
browser's path: sign in through the consent and get a session, read the
public routes (the release index, a manifest with its immutable headers,
the OpenAPI document byte-identical to the committed one, a 404 problem),
check a name, create an instance and read its plan, be refused
provisioning without an authorization, authorize, list zones, and
provision. Provisioning uploads the agent bundle to the stub account, and
the lane asserts its metadata: the modules, the Durable Object migration,
the ownership tags, the minted token's policies, and the secrets the
upload carried.

Those secrets are what the second worker boots with: the driver starts
the agent under wrangler with the instance id and the key the control
plane minted, exactly as the account would run it. From there the lane
proves the agent's side: health, CORS for the control plane's origin, the
agent API refusing a missing or wrong bearer, a forged grant and a name
outside the grant refused, the real grant accepted, and the converge that
follows: the product worker uploaded with the right bindings and the
completion token, the secrets landing in the account and appearing in
neither the control plane's log nor its event log, the schedule, the
bucket, the namespace, the domain, the assets, the probes, and the
instance reaching ready, with the WebSocket relay having carried the
steps. Then a configuration change previews and applies with
`keep_bindings` and no secret value in the upload; a rotation sets one
secret with no upload; and an uninstall is refused without a fresh
authorization, then tears down the worker, namespace, and domain, keeps
the bucket until the name is typed at the agent (a wrong name answers
`name_mismatch`), deletes it once typed, and ends with the agent worker
gone and its token revoked.

Run it: `just workerd`. It builds the bundles first.
EOF

cat > docs/adr/0001-the-deployer-is-its-own-repository.md <<'EOF'
# 0001: The deployer is its own repository and knows no product

## Decision

The deployer lives in its own repository. It owns the manifest schema, the
engine, the two workers, and the client, and it contains no knowledge of
any product. Each product emits its own manifest from its own repository
and publishes it to the deployer's release store.

## Reason

Sesame needs a Hyperdrive configuration, a `send_email` binding, and a
Postgres connection string the customer supplies; cachet needs an R2
bucket and a browser-made Ed25519 key; a later product may need something
else again. All of that is expressed in the product's manifest, and a
deployer that read product-specific code would need a release for every
product change. Keeping the deployer generic also keeps its trust boundary
small: it renders templates and applies them, and the product's own
repository is where the product's questions are asked and its grammar is
enforced.

## Ruled out

A `deployer` directory inside cachet's repository, which would have made
sesame depend on cachet.
EOF
cat > docs/adr/0002-rust-with-workers-rs-and-http-json.md <<'EOF'
# 0002: Rust with workers-rs; the client speaks HTTP JSON and one WebSocket

## Decision

The control plane and the agent are workers-rs workers, and the engine is
a plain Rust crate all three Rust consumers share (the agent, the control
plane, and a product's own CLI). The client talks to the control plane
over HTTP JSON described with utoipa and drift-gated, plus one hibernatable
WebSocket per instance for the event stream.

## Reason

One engine in one language means the render and apply logic has one home,
and a product's CLI can install without the service by depending on the
same crate. workers-rs's RPC support is experimental, covers
worker-to-worker calls over service bindings with primitive arguments, and
offers nothing for a browser, so it is not used; HTTP JSON with a generated
OpenAPI document is what the client can decode at its boundary.

## Ruled out

Cap'n Web or another RPC layer for the browser, and a TypeScript control
plane beside a Rust engine.
EOF
cat > docs/adr/0003-the-agent-runs-in-the-customers-account.md <<'EOF'
# 0003: The agent runs in the customer's account under an account-owned token

## Decision

A small agent worker per instance runs in the customer's account under an
account-owned API token minted during provisioning. It reads desired state
from the control plane, verifies and applies releases, takes secrets from
the browser, and reports every step. The control plane holds a customer's
access token only for the minutes an operation takes and never a refresh
token.

## Reason

Updating a product means writing into the account. If the control plane
did that itself it would need a standing credential for every customer
account, which is the largest possible blast radius for a compromise of
the service. An agent in the account holds a token scoped to that account
and that product, and the control plane holds nothing it could use later.
The agent's token lives where its work is.

## Ruled out

Folding the agent into the product worker, which would put an
account-write token beside the surface that parses untrusted input, and a
control plane that keeps refresh tokens.
EOF
cat > docs/adr/0004-secrets-go-browser-to-agent-under-grants.md <<'EOF'
# 0004: Secrets go from the browser to the agent under signed grants

## Decision

The browser posts a customer's secrets straight to the agent's URL over
TLS, authenticated by a short-lived grant the control plane signs naming
the instance, the purpose, and the secret names. The control plane relays
nothing secret and stores nothing secret. The agent holds the values until
the upload that carries them succeeds, then deletes them.

## Reason

cachet's signing key is the deployment's identity, and whoever can sign a
narinfo can execute code on every machine that substitutes from the cache.
A service that never holds the key cannot leak it. The grant is what lets
the agent know the post comes from the instance's owner acting now, and a
grant that names the secrets is what keeps a replay from setting anything
the person did not intend.

## Ruled out

Secrets posted to the control plane and forwarded, however briefly, and a
long-lived shared secret between browser and agent.
EOF
cat > docs/adr/0005-releases-are-signed-and-the-agent-verifies.md <<'EOF'
# 0005: Releases are signed by the product and verified by the agent

## Decision

A product's CI signs its published manifest with the product's release key,
over the bytes as published. The agent verifies the signature under the
product's public keys before it reads the manifest, and verifies every
module's hash before it uploads. The control plane carries public keys only.

## Reason

This is what draws the trust boundary the whole design rests on. A
compromised control plane can choose among published releases and change
configuration; it cannot install code nobody signed. Signing the bytes as
published, rather than a canonical form, means the two sides need agree on
nothing but the file.

## Ruled out

Unsigned releases trusted because they came from the control plane, and a
canonical-JSON signature scheme with two serializers to keep in step.
EOF
cat > docs/adr/0006-authorization-is-per-operation-with-no-refresh.md <<'EOF'
# 0006: An operation's authorization is held briefly and never refreshed

## Decision

Sign-in asks Cloudflare for the identity scopes and yields a session; the
identity token is revoked once the session exists. An operation inside an
account (provisioning, uninstalling, listing zones) asks for the write
scopes on that account as a second consent. The access token it yields is
held on the user's record until it expires or the operation ends, and for
a teardown a copy is held on the instance until the agent reports the
worker gone. `offline_access` is never requested.

## Reason

A refresh token is a standing credential for someone else's account. An
access token an hour long, dropped when the work is done, is the smallest
thing that can still do the work. Holding it on the user's record rather
than only in a request lets the wizard use one consent for the name check,
the zone list, and the deploy, and lets a teardown finish after the agent
has done its part.

## Ruled out

Refresh tokens, and a control plane that acts in accounts on a schedule
without the person present.
EOF
cat > docs/adr/0007-ownership-is-a-tag-and-collisions-are-classified.md <<'EOF'
# 0007: Ownership is a tag on the worker, and pre-flight classifies collisions

## Decision

Every worker the engine uploads carries tags naming the instance, the
product, the release, and the manifest schema. Before anything is created,
pre-flight reads the tags under the plan's worker name and classifies what
is there: absent, this instance's, another instance's, a newer deployer's,
or not deployed here. Only the first two proceed.

## Reason

Names are deterministic, which is what makes every step idempotent, and a
deterministic name can collide with something a person made by hand or
with another instance. Overwriting silently would be the worst outcome; a
refusal that names what is there and what to do is a step in the list like
any other. The schema tag keeps an older deployer from rewriting a worker a
newer one manages.

## Ruled out

A state store that remembers what the deployer created, which is what
alchemy kept and what made a lost state file a deployment problem.
EOF
cat > docs/adr/0008-the-control-plane-chooses-the-version-the-agent-applies-it.md <<'EOF'
# 0008: Automatic updates: the control plane chooses, the agent applies

## Decision

An instance with automatic updates on is moved to the promoted release by
the control plane's hourly alarm once the release has been promoted for
the instance's delay; the agent then applies it in the account like any
other change to desired state. The agent applies its own promoted release
to itself, once per promoted version.

## Reason

The control plane already knows what is promoted and when, and it already
may choose among signed releases (ADR 0005); an agent choosing on its own
would leave desired state stale and two places deciding. The applying stays
in the account because that is where the token is. A per-instance delay is
what lets a customer's own staging instance meet a release before their
production one does.

## Ruled out

An agent that reads the release feed and moves itself without the control
plane recording the move.
EOF
cat > docs/adr/0009-the-client-is-the-consoles-sibling.md <<'EOF'
# 0009: The client is the console's sibling, with one colour rule changed

## Decision

The client reuses cachet's console foundation: the tokens, the primitives,
the segmented control, the format helpers, and the frame. It adds what a
wizard needs (fields with verdicts, choices, a step list, a confirm dialog,
pills, a copy control, a key pair display). One rule changes: the signal
colour is for a failed step, a refused input, and an armed destructive
button, and for nothing that succeeded.

## Reason

Two nox products in one system read as one system, and the console's
choices (square corners, hairlines, dense facts, no explanations beside
numbers) were made for exactly this kind of screen. The console paints a
healthy status red because its only red is a status dot; a deploy flow has
many success states, and a step list where done is red reads as failure.

## Ruled out

A component library with its own styling system, and a second visual
language for the same company's second product.
EOF
cat > docs/adr/0010-authorization-is-the-wizards-second-step.md <<'EOF'
# 0010: Authorization is the wizard's second step, before any secret

## Decision

The wizard asks for the Cloudflare authorization right after the product
and account are chosen, before the name, the configuration, and the
secrets. The non-secret draft is kept in the browser's session storage
across the redirect; secrets are typed afterwards and kept in memory only.

## Reason

The authorization is a full-page redirect through Cloudflare's consent
page, and a secret typed before it would have to survive that navigation
in some storage the page can read back. Nothing that holds a secret may
outlive the page. Authorizing early also gives the name check and the
zone picker the account access they need.

## Ruled out

Authorizing as the last step, which the first plan drew, and storing
secrets in session storage across the redirect.
EOF

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

            --var OAUTH_CLIENT_ID:"$OAUTH_CLIENT_ID" \

# --var and the secrets (OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET, CONTROL_SIGNING_SEED) live in

name = "deployer-control"
compatibility_date = "2026-05-01"
main = "build/index.js"

[observability]

[[kv_namespaces]]

[[r2_buckets]]

[durable_objects]

  { name = "INSTANCES", class_name = "InstanceObject" },
  { name = "RELEASE_INDEX", class_name = "ReleaseIndex" },
]

[[migrations]]

[assets]

run_worker_first = true
html_handling = "none"
not_found_handling = "none"
EOF
